100.summary: A craftsperson who made lanterns from bamboo strips and washi paper. As lighting became electric, the lantern's role shifted from 'light source' to 'symbol.'
body: They would coil bamboo strips into a spiral frame, paste washi paper onto it, dry it, and remove it from the mold. Characters and family crests were hand-painted. Lanterns were produced in large quantities as everyday lighting fixtures, and also as markers for shop names and festivals. Their collapsible structure was a masterpiece of Japanese lighting, combining practicality with beauty.

timeline.text: Electric lights become widespread in homes and on streets
The lantern's role as a light source ends
Survives for festivals, signage, and decoration

100.timelineClose: It ceased to be a 'tool for illumination' and became a 'symbol representing Japaneseness.' This is a transformed profession that survived by shifting its purpose from practical use to symbolic representation.
100.trivia: The red lanterns at izakayas are lit not as illumination, but as a symbol indicating 'this is a shop.' Lantern makers transitioned from creating light to creating meaning.
100.lineageText: Lantern Maker → Electric Lighting (survives for festivals and signage)

101.summary: A craftsperson who made umbrellas from bamboo, washi paper, and oil. They largely lost their market due to the import and domestic production of Western-style umbrellas.
body: They would split bamboo to create dozens of ribs, paste washi paper onto them, and apply perilla oil for waterproofing. The number of ribs could be several dozen, all made by hand. A precise structure for opening and closing, with ribs bundled by a component called a 'rokuro' (runner), was supported by a collective of specialized artisans. The beauty of the umbrella when opened was part of its appeal.

timeline.text: Western-style umbrellas (kōmorigasa) are imported
Lightweight, durable, and inexpensive Western-style umbrellas are domestically produced and mass-produced
A few survive as craft items, for stage use, and for tea ceremony

101.timelineClose: It couldn't compete with Western-style umbrellas, which offered lightness, affordability, and durability—a triple threat. However, on the single point of 'beauty,' wagasa survived as a craft.
101.trivia: Wagasa production was based on a division of labor, with rib-making, paper-pasting, and oil-coating handled by different artisans. Because the entire production area worked together to create a single umbrella, if one person was missing, the whole process would halt—division of labor creates efficiency but also fragility.
101.lineageText: Wagasa Umbrella Maker → Western Umbrella (survives for crafts and stage use)

102.quote: i'll patch up your pot's hole
102.summary: A repairman who traveled around, welding and fixing pots and kettles with holes on the spot. They were defeated by an era where 'buying was better than repairing.'
body: Carrying bellows and charcoal fire on a shoulder pole, they would walk through alleys, calling out 'Ikake-ya~' to attract customers. They would take pots and kettles with holes, light a charcoal fire on the spot, and seal the holes with molten metal. The repair would be done in a few tens of minutes, and the pot could be used for many more years. They were a pillar of the circular economy in an era when metal was precious.

timeline.text: Inexpensive aluminum and stainless steel pots are mass-produced
'Replace when broken' becomes the norm
The repair economy disappears

102.timelineClose: A new item became cheaper than the cost of repair—at that moment, the repair business ceased to be viable. This is an example of a pricing structure, not technology, killing a profession.
102.trivia: In recent years, the culture of repairing and continuing to use items has been re-evaluated in the context of sustainability, and the 'right to repair' is being debated globally. The very pricing structure that eliminated the tinker is now being questioned.
102.lineageText: Tinker → Disposable/Replacement Culture → (Towards the 'Right to Repair' debate)

103.quote: change the teeth, and you can still wear them
103.summary: A super-sustainable repair service that replaced only the worn-out 'teeth' of geta clogs. The profession vanished when the footwear itself disappeared.
body: They would remove worn-out teeth from geta clogs and insert new ones, leaving the base intact. The teeth were shaved to fit the holes in the base, ensuring a snug yet not too tight fit. In a few tens of minutes, the geta were as good as new. They conducted their business on street corners and in alleys, repairing on the spot.
tools: Eye for measuring the base's dimensions

timeline.text: Western shoes become everyday footwear
Geta disappear from daily life, and footwear culture changes
Demand for tooth replacement also vanishes

103.timelineClose: The design of replacing only the consumable parts was a clever construction, predicated on repair. But if the product itself disappears from daily life, even the most excellent repair service cannot survive.
103.trivia: Geta were footwear designed with the philosophy that 'if only the teeth are replaced, the base can be used for a lifetime.' This idea of extending lifespan through modular replacement is the same thinking behind today's repair-friendly gadget designs.

104.summary: A craftsperson who cleaned and replaced the bamboo stems (rao) of kiseru pipes. They vanished along with the product itself.
body: They would load a small steam boiler onto a handcart or stall and roam the streets. They cleaned kiseru bamboo stems clogged with tar by passing steam through them, and replaced damaged stems with new bamboo. The call 'Raou-ya~' and the 'shuu' sound of steam were their signals for business. Kiseru pipes were tools meant to be used for a lifetime, and the rao pipe repairer extended that lifespan.

timeline.text: Rolled cigarettes become widespread
Kiseru pipe smoking rapidly declines
Demand for rao pipe repairers vanishes entirely

104.timelineClose: The maintenance profession for a tool is entirely subservient to the fate of the tool itself. If the kiseru disappears, so too does the rao pipe repairer—it was an unavoidable extinction.
104.trivia: Rao pipe repairers announced their arrival with the sound of steam. A business that operated solely by sound, without a vocal call, held a unique presence within the urban soundscape.
104.lineageText: Rao Pipe Repairer → Rolled Cigarettes → Electronic Cigarettes

105.summary: Men whose job it was to wash customers' backs at public bathhouses. This iconic profession, a fixture of bathhouses since the Edo period, survived the era of private baths and persisted until the end of the Heisei era.
body: When a customer requested a 'wash' at the counter, they'd receive a wooden tag, and a call of 'wash-ee!' would echo into the bathing area. The Sansuke would kneel behind the customer, scrub their back with a towel and soap, massage their shoulders, and finish by rinsing them with hot water. It was a craft of the palms, where the right amount of pressure and rhythm were everything.

Originally, Sansuke were servants who handled all the heavy labor in a public bathhouse, such as stoking the furnace, adjusting water temperature, and managing footwear. Washing backs was their star service. They were both the unsung heroes and the main attraction supporting Edo's bathhouse culture.

timeline.text: Public bathhouses themselves began to decline with the spread of private home baths.
Public bathhouses employing Sansuke became few and far between.
The 'last Sansuke' working in a Tokyo public bathhouse retired.

105.timelineClose: When baths moved inside homes, the stranger who would wash your back vanished from daily life. The retirement of the last one was reported in newspapers—a profession whose 'date of demise' is recorded.
105.trivia: One theory suggests the name 'Sansuke' comes from 'assisting three things': tending the fire for heating water, adjusting the water temperature, and washing backs. In the Edo period, strong and cheerful Sansuke were popular figures in town, known as a profession that attracted many admirers.
105.lineageText: Sansuke → Private home baths → Super sento body scrubbing/massage

106.summary: Japanese ice sellers who delivered ice for iceboxes. Their quiet end came in the 1960s (Showa 40s), when refrigerator penetration exceeded 90%.
body: They would procure large ice blocks from ice factories and deliver them by handcart or bicycle. According to orders, they would cut the ice with a saw, carry it with ice tongs, and place it in the upper compartment of each household's wooden 'icebox.' Daily in summer, every few days in winter. They also retailed ice for shaved ice, and the 'Ice' flag outside their shops was a summer tradition.

timeline.text: Electric refrigerators began to spread in homes.
Refrigerator penetration exceeded 90%.
Demand for ice delivery disappeared.

106.timelineClose: They met the same fate as American ice deliverymen (No. 024), albeit at a different time. The same technology sequentially eliminates the same profession across different countries.
106.trivia: Shaved ice made from ice seller's ice remains a summer tradition today. The job of 'delivering' ice vanished, but the job of 'shaving and selling' ice survived.
106.lineageText: Ice harvester → Ice deliveryman → Ice seller → Electric refrigerator

107.summary: A mobile vendor who sold steamed buns from a cart pulled by a donkey (though horses were more common). Children would gather, drawn by the music.
body: They would load steamed buns onto a small cart pulled by a donkey or horse and tour residential areas, playing music. When the 'Donkey Man's' theme song was heard, children would run out, clutching their coins. More than just selling bread, they brought a small event to the streets, a combination of animals, music, and sweet aromas.

timeline.text: Bakeries and supermarkets became everyday shopping destinations.
Changes in traffic conditions made it impossible for animal-drawn carts to operate in the streets.
Mobile bread vendors disappeared.

107.timelineClose: A business that sold experiences rather than just products was defeated by stores where products alone could be purchased efficiently. However, what remained in memory was not the taste, but that music.
107.trivia: The Donkey Bread Cart's music serves as a powerful memory trigger for the generation who heard it. The style of playing music in the streets to sell goods is still carried on today by baked sweet potato vendors and recycling trucks.
107.lineageText: Donkey bread cart → Mass-market bakeries/convenience stores

108.summary: A mobile processing business that gathered children with a 'pop!' explosion sound. If you brought rice, they would transform it into a snack on the spot.
body: Rice was placed in a pressure cooker and heated; once the pressure built up, it was released all at once. With a thunderous 'pop!', the puffed rice would burst out, becoming 'pon-gashi' (puffed rice). It was also a service business where customers brought their own rice to be processed for a fee. The moment children covered their ears and braced themselves for the announced explosion was the show itself.

timeline.text: Mass production and distribution of sweets made cheap candies available in stores.
Demand for mobile processing businesses decreased.
Survives as event demonstrations and local specialties.

108.timelineClose: Though it vanished as an everyday business, it survived as an event performance, offering the experiential value of 'sound and live demonstration.' A classic example of extended life through entertainment.
108.trivia: The puffed rice machine, despite its simple principle of puffing rice, attracted people with its spectacular performance. Even when the same product became available in stores, that sound could not be bought.
108.lineageText: Puffed rice maker → Mass-market sweets (survives as event demonstrations)

109.summary: He carried a stage on his bicycle, clapped wooden blocks to gather children, and narrated picture stories while selling starch syrup candy. He was the 'street video streamer' of his time.
body: He would insert pictures into a wooden frame on his bicycle's carrier, clap wooden blocks to gather children in an empty lot. Children who bought starch syrup or cheap sweets could sit in the front row; candy sales were his income, and kamishibai was his means of attracting customers. He'd use different voices and cut off the story at a crucial point with 'The rest is tomorrow!' His skill lay in his narrative structure, designed to make them return the next day.

timeline.text: Television broadcasting began.
Television spread to homes, and children moved from empty lots to living rooms.
Street kamishibai disappeared.

109.timelineClose: The sound of wooden blocks couldn't compete with moving pictures that could be watched for free at home. However, many kamishibai artists and writers transitioned into the world of TV anime and manga.
109.trivia: Many talents who would later support Japan's manga and anime industries emerged from kamishibai creators. Personnel from an industry destroyed by television moved to the side that created television content—its demise was also a migration of talent.
109.lineageText: Peep show → Katsudō benshi → Kamishibai man → Television → Streamer

110.summary: During the era when movies had no sound, this was a storytelling profession where a performer stood beside the screen and single-handedly voiced characters and narrated the story. Japanese silent films were considered a complete work only when paired with a benshi.
body: When a screening began, the benshi would stand at a podium beside the screen. They would narrate the plot, skillfully differentiate voices for male and female roles, and sometimes even add lines not present in the film to entertain the audience. Paired with live musical accompaniment, they transformed each film into a unique 'live' performance every time.

Popular benshi were as famous as movie stars, and many patrons chose movie theaters specifically to see 'that benshi's show.' Even with the same film, a different benshi meant a different movie. Half of the right to interpret the work was held by the benshi.

timeline.text: The world's first talkie, 'The Jazz Singer,' was released.
Japanese cinemas also switched to talkies, leading to mass unemployment and disputes among benshi.
A few active benshi perform at silent film screenings.

110.timelineClose: When movies began to speak for themselves, there was no longer a need for someone to speak on their behalf. Unemployed benshi scattered into roles as stand-up comedians, kamishibai men, and later, voice actors and narrators. Technology took their voices, but the artisans of voice survived on different stages.
110.trivia: It is said that popular benshi at their peak earned higher salaries than movie studio executives. This profession is often cited in recent discussions about 'what if AI takes our jobs' because it's a precedent where the job didn't disappear but transformed into voice acting and narration.
110.lineageText: Peep show → Katsudō benshi → Voice actor/Narrator → AI voice synthesis ▲Under discussion

111.quote: i draw big billboards by hand
111.summary: Artists who hand-painted the giant billboards adorning the front of movie theaters. Large-format printing made them put down their brushes.
body: They would enlarge and paint actors' faces onto plywood boards several meters square, using still photographs as reference. In addition to portraiture skills, they needed a sense of color and composition that would look striking from a distance. Since billboards were repainted for each new screening, the cityscape would change every few weeks. The quality of the billboard directly influenced attendance; it was the frontline of attracting customers.

timeline.text: Large-format photographic printing became inexpensive and high-quality.
With the rise of multiplex cinemas, nationally standardized posters were used.
Hand-painted billboards disappeared from the streets.

111.timelineClose: The accuracy of photographs and the cost-efficiency of national standardization prevailed over the charm of hand-painting. Billboards transformed from 'the work of a local artist' to 'printed material from a distribution company.'
111.trivia: In the past, billboard designs differed from cinema to cinema, so the same movie had a different 'face' depending on the town. The room for local interpretation vanished with the spread of printing.
111.lineageText: Cinema billboard painter → Large-format printed posters

112.summary: A human advertising medium that paraded through the streets with musical instruments and costumes, promoting shops. A small number still exist as entertainers.
body: They would walk through the streets in flamboyant costumes and white makeup, playing instruments like chindon drums, clarinets, and shamisen. They would announce new openings and sales, distribute flyers, and deliver promotional speeches. They were professionals at attracting attention—making people turn with sound and remember with their appearance. They were an agile medium, adapting to the advertising budgets of local shops.

timeline.text: TV commercials and newspaper inserts became the main forms of advertising.
The efficiency of street advertising relatively declined.
A small number operate as entertainers/event performers.

112.timelineClose: Advertising budgets shifted to broadcast media and print, making street performance less cost-effective. However, in recent years, there's been a movement to re-evaluate them in the context of 'buzz' that spreads on social media.
112.trivia: The sound of chindon-ya was 'unignorable advertising.' You couldn't skip it or block it; if you walked the streets, you were bound to hear it—the ideal form of advertising, surprisingly, existed on street corners a century ago.
112.lineageText: Chindon-ya → Advertising agencies/SNS advertising (survives as entertainment)

113.quote: i wonder if this suits me
113.summary: A 'living advertisement' who wore and displayed products in stores. The prototype of the dispatched sales associate.
body: In department stores and at special events, they would wear and display clothes and cosmetics to customers, explain them, and make sales. More than just a substitute for a mannequin, they were customer service professionals who proposed styling ideas and answered questions. In the early Showa era, it was a modern profession that embodied the latest fashion, drawing attention and becoming an object of admiration in the city.

timeline.text: Department store sales associates become an established, common profession.
Their role is absorbed by manufacturer-dispatched sales associates and demonstrators.
The term 'mannequin girl' disappears.

113.timelineClose: Rather than the profession disappearing, its name and special status vanished. When it became a job anyone could do, its professional title was relegated to history.
113.trivia: The word 'mannequin' originates from the French 'mannequin' (model doll). Because people stood in place of dolls, they were called 'living mannequins.' It's a rare example of a name derived from a doll becoming the title of a human profession.

114.quote: shall i fill it up for you?
114.summary: Women who handled customer service and refueling at gas stations. Self-service was a precursor to automated checkouts, and the fate of this job is a preview for cashiers (NO.142).
body: At gas stations, they would greet customers' cars, refuel them, wipe windows, and check oil levels. In the early Showa era, gas stations where women in modern uniforms served customers were a new urban sight and garnered much attention. It wasn't just about refueling; it was about selling the 'hospitality' that accompanied the new luxury item: the automobile.

timeline.text: Gas stations change due to gasoline rationing and other factors.
The shift from full-service to self-service begins.
Self-service gas stations are legalized in Japan*.

114.timelineClose: Human-served refueling was replaced by customer self-service refueling. The same structural change is now happening at checkouts.
114.trivia: When self-service refueling was legalized, there were debates about whether it would be 'dangerous' or 'inconvenient.' But within a few years, it became commonplace. Current debates surrounding self-checkouts might similarly be forgotten in 20 years.
114.lineageText: Street vendor → Peddler → Gasoline girl → Cashier → Self-checkout / Unmanned store

115.summary: Women who served customers in 'cafés' from the Taisho to Showa eras. A profession symbolizing the light and shadow of Taisho Modernism.
body: In Western-style eateries called 'cafés,' they would sit beside customers, pour drinks, and engage in conversation. Many operated on an unstable system with no fixed salary, relying on tips from customers as their income. While admired as a modern profession, it also faced social criticism as a moral issue. It frequently appeared as a subject in literary works.

timeline.text: Public morality regulations are strengthened.
Business types are differentiated and reorganized with the establishment of the Entertainment Business Act.
The terms 'café' and 'café waitress' disappear.

115.timelineClose: Business types were legally organized, separating into coffee shops, bars, and cabarets. Rather than the profession disappearing, the system redrew its boundaries.
115.trivia: The 'café' of that era was an entirely different business from today's 'café,' focusing more on alcohol and customer interaction than coffee. It's an example of the same word completely changing its meaning over time.
115.lineageText: Café waitress → Coffee shop / Hospitality industry (business differentiation)

116.quote: i'll write it for you, anything at all
116.summary: A business that wrote documents on behalf of others, often in front of government offices. A rare case of 'evolving into a national qualification' rather than disappearing.
body: In an era when literacy rates were not sufficient, they would write applications for government offices, contracts, letters, and more on behalf of customers. Beyond just being able to write, they needed knowledge of formats and laws, and many set up shop right in front of government offices. Knowing how to write documents was, in itself, a specialization.
tools: location in front of government offices

timeline.text: The number of people who 'cannot write' decreases with improved literacy rates.
A qualification system is established for administrative scriveners and judicial scriveners.
Unqualified scrivener work is absorbed into the system.

116.timelineClose: The job of writing characters disappeared, but the expertise in handling documents was institutionalized as a qualification. This is a rare case of 'promotion' rather than 'extinction'.
116.trivia: The Rakugo performance 'Daisho' (Scrivener) is a hilarious story depicting the interaction between an illiterate customer and a scrivener. A vanished profession lives on the stage as a record of laughter.
116.lineageText: Scrivener → Administrative scrivener / Judicial scrivener (national qualification)

117.quote: rags and scraps, anything to clear out~
117.summary: A collection business that managed urban resource circulation with just a bamboo basket. Only its philosophy has returned, as SDGs.
body: With a cry of 'Rags and scraps, anything to clear out~,' they would go around alleys, buying old paper, rags, metal scraps, bottles, and more. The collected items were sold to wholesalers and recycled as raw materials. It was a business of buying resources, not trash, with individuals handling the final stage of urban material circulation. Knowledge of market prices and a keen eye were their trade skills.

timeline.text: The relative value of resources decreases due to mass production and mass consumption.
Municipal sorted waste collection is institutionalized.
From individual buying businesses to government and the recycling industry.

117.timelineClose: The 'people who bought trash' disappeared, and a 'system for discarding trash' emerged. And now, the philosophy of circulating resources is reappearing under the name of SDGs—the waste collector has been resurrected as an idea.
117.trivia: From the Edo period to the Showa era, Japanese cities were thorough recycling societies. Paper scrap buyers, ash buyers, used clothing stores—almost everything found a buyer. A circular economy is not a new ideal, but a former standard.
117.lineageText: Rag buyer → Waste collector → Scrap collection → Recycling industry

118.quote: it'll become fertilizer for the fields
118.summary: The job of collecting night soil from pit toilets. Once, night soil was a 'marketable product' as fertilizer, and its collectors were key players in the circular economy.
body: They would scoop night soil from toilets with a dipper and bucket, then transport the buckets with a carrying pole or cart. In the Edo period, farmers would buy it in exchange for money or vegetables, making urban night soil a valuable fertilizer resource. It was so valuable that collection rights were bought and sold, becoming a significant source of income for landlords.

timeline.text: The value of night soil as fertilizer disappears with the spread of chemical fertilizers.
Sewer systems and flush toilets become widespread.
Demand for night soil collection drastically decreases.

118.timelineClose: What was once 'bought' became something for which 'money was paid to dispose of.' The moment a resource plummeted to waste, the meaning of the profession handling it also inverted.
118.trivia: The city of Edo maintained one of the world's highest levels of cleanliness because there was a system where night soil was bought and sold as a resource and transported to rural areas. Urban sanitation was supported not by sewers, but by economics.
118.lineageText: Night soil collector → Sewer systems + Chemical fertilizers

119.summary: A byword for post-war street corners. They lined up boxes in front of stations and shined shoes. Now, it's subtly reappearing as a craft, costing several thousand yen per pair.
body: They would pack their tools into a wooden box, sit on the streets in front of stations or in bustling districts, and wait for customers. They'd brush off dust, apply cream, and polish with a cloth. In minutes, the leather would be revived. During the chaotic post-war period, it was a means of survival for war orphans and the unemployed, and an integral part of the streetscape.

timeline.text: The demand for leather shoes decreases with the rise of sneakers and casualization.
Regulations on street vending also progress.
Partially revived as a luxury shoeshine service.

119.timelineClose: It disappeared as an everyday essential service, only to return as a luxury experiential service. The same craft survived by changing its price and location.
119.trivia: Many post-war shoeshiners were children, and their image is etched into songs and films of the era. A job that was a last resort for survival has now become a luxury service—the same action, with opposite meanings.

120.quote: read it, then return it, okay?
120.summary: A business that rented out books for a fee. It was a relay point in the 'borrowing culture' lineage: rental shops → book rental shops → video rental → streaming.
body: They would display books in their shops or carry them on their backs, visiting regular customers, renting out a book for a few days at a certain price. In an era when books were expensive, it was the only way for common people to access stories. In the Showa era, a large number of comics were drawn exclusively for rental shops, forming a unique publishing market. Many manga artists emerged from this scene.

timeline.text: Weekly manga magazines and inexpensive paperback books become widespread.
Development of public libraries progresses.
Book rental shops disappear.

120.timelineClose: It disappeared, caught between 'being able to buy cheaply' and 'being able to borrow for free.' However, the demand for 'borrowing' itself did not die, but was passed on to video rentals, and then to subscriptions.
120.trivia: Many artists who would later support Japan's manga industry emerged from rental manga. A vanished distribution format had cultivated the soil of Japanese culture.
120.lineageText: Rental shop → Book rental shop → Video rental → Subscription streaming

121.summary: These street performers played the violin, sang songs, and sold lyric sheets on city streets. The very word 'enka' originates from this profession.
body: They earned a living by playing the violin on bustling city streets, singing about current events and social trends, and selling songbooks (lyric sheets). The origin lies in 'enzetsu-ka' (speech-songs), political speeches from the Freedom and People's Rights Movement set to music, which was then abbreviated to 'enka'. The song was the medium, the street was the stage, and the songbook was the product.

timeline.text: Records and radio take over song distribution
Singers become a profession of 'selling records'
The business of selling songbooks on the street disappears

121.timelineClose: The means of delivering songs shifted from human voice to discs and radio waves. Yet, the word 'enka' alone survives, as the name of an entirely different genre.
121.trivia: Today's 'enka' refers to a genre of popular song, but its etymology is the political 'enzetsu-ka' (speech-song). Only the word remains, its meaning completely transformed. Names outlive professions, sometimes changing their very essence.
121.lineageText: Bard → Enka street singer → Record singer → Streaming

122.summary: Carrying guitars or accordions, they toured bars, playing requests for patrons. Karaoke machines eventually stole their audience.
body: They would visit one drinking establishment after another at night, asking, 'Would you like a song?' When a customer named a tune, they would provide accompaniment on the spot. With a vast repertoire memorized and the ability to instantly adapt to any key, their skill in making customers sing comfortably directly translated into their income.

timeline.text: Karaoke spreads in bars
The emergence of karaoke boxes changes where people sing
A very small number of nagashi remain active

122.timelineClose: Machines don't tire, are cheap, and provide accompaniment anytime. However, machines don't look at a customer's face and change the key—it's that very difference that allows some nagashi to still exist today.
122.trivia: Not a few singers rose to fame from being nagashi. Their daily rounds through bars served as a de facto audition. Vanished professions were also mechanisms for discovering talent.

123.quote: i wonder if there's work today
123.summary: Day laborers who worked in post-war unemployment relief projects. Their daily wage of 240 yen—'nikoyon' (two-four-zero)—became their very name.
body: Each morning, they gathered at the public employment office and were assigned work for the day: road construction, cleaning, miscellaneous civil engineering tasks, and so on. Their daily wage was 240 yen (ni-ko-yon, literally 'two-four'). Institutionalized as a public works project to aid the unemployed, it supported the lives of many during the chaotic post-war period. Whether there would be work or not was unknown until that very morning.

timeline.text: Unemployment rate falls with rapid economic growth
Unemployment relief projects are gradually scaled back and abolished
The name itself becomes a thing of the past

123.timelineClose: Economic growth eliminated this profession by making it 'unnecessary.' A disappearance due to a reduction in misfortune—a welcome extinction.
123.trivia: The name 'nikoyon' is a rare example where a wage amount became the profession's name itself. The prices of the era and the memory of labor are encapsulated in a single word.

124.summary: Boys who lived and worked as apprentices in merchant households. Labor laws and compulsory education brought an end to this system.
body: Around the age of 10, they would live in a merchant's house, learning the trade by starting with cleaning and errands. There was virtually no salary; their compensation was room and board, and the future prospect of 'noren-wake' (being allowed to open a branch shop). After several years, they would be promoted to clerk (tedai) and then manager (banto), eventually being permitted to become independent—it was also a long-term human resource development system. Strict discipline and long working hours were prerequisites.

timeline.text: Labor Standards Act restricts child labor
Thorough implementation of compulsory education sends children to school
The apprentice system becomes unviable

124.timelineClose: The training model of 'using cheaply and for a long time, eventually rewarding' was prohibited by law. The philosophy of human resource development persists, transformed into new graduate recruitment and in-house training.
124.trivia: The path from apprentice to manager and then independence bears a strong resemblance to the modern 'new graduate hire to independent entrepreneur.' Even if the system vanishes, the archetype of the career narrative lives on.
124.lineageText: Apprentice boy → New graduate recruitment / Internships

125.summary: A trade that peddled 'Goshin'ei' (portraits of the Emperor). It vanished overnight with a change in the political system.
body: They would frame portraits of the Emperor and Empress and sell them door-to-door to homes and shops. Before the war, displaying a Goshin'ei was an expression of patriotism, and there was an atmosphere that demanded they be displayed in homes. Schools had 'Hoan-den' (reverence halls) where the photographs were treated as sacred. The demand was supported not by the product's intrinsic value, but by the national sentiment of the era.

timeline.text: National system changes due to defeat in war
The Emperor's declaration of humanity and democratization of education change the status of Goshin'ei
Demand completely vanishes

125.timelineClose: Though the product itself remained unchanged, its meaning was rewritten by politics, and the market evaporated. Demand created by the state can disappear in a single day if the state changes.
125.trivia: Goshin'ei were treated as the most important objects in schools, and in case of fire, one was expected to risk one's life to retrieve them. This is a record of an era where not the object itself, but the meaning ascribed to it, was considered more precious than human life.
125.lineageText: Imperial portrait seller → (Vanished with regime change)

126.summary: Merchants who illegally distributed goods under a controlled economy. It vanished for a rare reason: 'economic normalization.'
body: During and after the war, in an era when rations alone were insufficient, they procured rice and vegetables from rural areas and sold them at exorbitant prices in cities. Carrying backpacks, they rode trains and evaded police crackdowns. Though illegal, without the black markets, urban residents would have starved. It was a distribution system that broke the law, yet sustained lives.

timeline.text: Material controls are eased by economic stabilization policies
Legitimate distribution recovers, eliminating the need for the black market
Black markets disappear, and some merchants move to legitimate stores

126.timelineClose: Professions born of abnormal times disappear when those times normalize. Many black markets became the prototypes for today's shopping streets and station-front markets—towns with illicit origins still remain in various places.
126.trivia: The anecdote of a judge who refused the black market, lived solely on rations, and died of malnutrition is well-known. Obey the law and die, break it and live—the existence of the black marketeer was the very contradiction of that era.
126.lineageText: Black marketeer → Recovery of legitimate distribution

127.quote: i turn bowls in the mountains
127.summary: A nomadic group of artisans who lived in the mountains, turning bowls and trays on a lathe. Everyday tableware was eventually taken over by plastic products.
body: They moved from mountain to mountain in search of good timber, felling trees on the spot and carving bowls and trays with a hand-powered lathe. Their nomadic life involved moving to the next mountain once the timber in one was exhausted. They held a tradition of being granted the privilege to freely traverse mountains across the country and formed their own unique communities.

timeline.text: Inexpensive plastic tableware becomes widely available
Privatization and regulation of forests make free movement difficult
Continues to exist as a settled traditional craft (e.g., lacquerware bases)

127.timelineClose: The shift in materials and the loss of freedom of movement—a nomadic profession vanished for a dual reason. The skill remained, but the way of life was lost first.
127.trivia: It is said that woodturners carried a historical document granting them permission from the Imperial Court to freely fell trees in mountains across the country. *A single piece of paper guaranteeing freedom of movement was the foundation of their livelihood.
127.lineageText: Woodturner → Resin products (continues as traditional craft)

128.summary: Artisans who measured floors and crafted tatami mats with not a single millimeter of error. Demand has shrunk due to the Westernization of homes.
body: They would measure room dimensions, attach an igusa (rush) surface to a straw core, and sew on the borders. Japanese houses often aren't perfect rectangles due to pillar distortions, so each mat had to be a different size. Reading these distortions and laying the mats without gaps was the artisan's skill. Replacing the tatami surface (omote-gae) was also a regular task.

timeline.text: Flooring becomes mainstream with the Westernization of homes
Machine sewing and factory production replace manual labor
Continues to exist, albeit in decline

128.timelineClose: When floors change, so do the floor artisans. Shifts in lifestyle gradually erode demand—it's not a sudden death, but a long, weakening transformation.
128.trivia: Rooms in Japanese houses were often not perfect rectangles, so tatami mats were made in different dimensions, one by one. Ready-made products wouldn't fit—that very fact necessitated the tatami maker's skill.
128.lineageText: Tatami maker → Machine production / Flooring (continues in decline)

129.summary: A port laborer who hammered rust off ship bottoms. Known as "kankan-mushi" (clang-clang bug) for the sound they made, this was the lowest-tier job in shipyards.
body: Clinging to the bottom of ships in dry dock, they would hammer and scrape off barnacles and rust. Their appearance, stuck to the hull, and the incessant 'clang-clang' sound earned them the nickname "kankan-mushi." It was simple labor under harsh conditions—dust, noise, heights—and many were day laborers.

timeline.text: High-pressure washing (water jet) becomes practical
Advances in antifouling paint reduce marine growth itself
Manual rust removal becomes unnecessary

129.timelineClose: Technology eliminated harsh labor—a desirable disappearance. However, whether a safety net was provided for those who relied on that work is another story.
129.trivia: The name "kankan-mushi" was a derogatory term, closer to a slur, given by others rather than the laborers themselves. Even the perspective embedded in a job title becomes a record of its era.
129.lineageText: Ship scaler → High-pressure washing / Antifouling paint

130.summary: Mass-market entertainment magazines made from poor-quality paper, which proliferated in the post-war ruins. One theory suggests their name came from the saying, "they'll go bust after three issues (san-go)," an publishing industry destined for a short life.
body: They procured cheap paper when controls were relaxed and filled magazines with content on sex, sensationalism, and true stories. Editing and writing were done by a small staff, printing was crude, and changing the magazine's title and reissuing it was common. If banned by authorities, they would simply launch a new title. It was a hand-to-mouth operation, supplying the entertainment sought by people in the war-torn cities as quickly as possible.

timeline.text: Proliferation due to relaxed censorship and lifting of paper controls
Major publishers' weekly magazines reclaim the entertainment market
The flood of crudely produced magazines disappears

130.timelineClose: When order returned to publishing, the businesses that could only thrive in disorder vanished. However, many writers and editors from this period went on to shape the later weekly magazine culture.
130.trivia: "Kastori" comes from the name of a crude, illicitly brewed shochu. A well-known theory suggests the magazine's name was a pun, meaning "you'd get drunk after three measures (san-go)." A rare industry that wove its own short lifespan into its name.
130.lineageText: Pulp magazine publisher → Weekly magazines / Entertainment publishing

131.summary: A lone wolf reporter who independently investigated scoops and sold them to magazines. The name comes from their aim to land the "top story" on a magazine's pages.
body: Not affiliated with any company, they would investigate incidents or newsworthy topics using their own sources and connections, then write articles and sell them to magazines. A hit meant big money; a miss meant no income. They paid their own expenses and needed strong sales skills to break into multiple weekly magazines. Their product wasn't an editorial plan, but solely their own nose for a story.

timeline.text: The weekly magazine boom sees freelance scoop reporters thrive
Magazines establish their own dedicated reporting teams and editorial structures
The practice of selling scoops on a buy-out basis declines

131.timelineClose: When publishers established systems to "create in-house," the space for external sellers narrowed. However, the lineage itself continues today in the form of freelance journalists.
131.trivia: Many journalists and writers started as freelance scoop reporters, and their investigative methods laid the groundwork for later investigative journalism. Reporters outside the system honed the journalism within organizations.
131.lineageText: Freelance scoop reporter → Freelance reporter / Investigative journalism

132.summary: Urgent news delivered even late at night with the cry of "Telegram!" Today, only the ceremonial use of congratulatory and condolence telegrams remains.
body: Upon receiving a telegram, they would rush to the recipient's address by bicycle or motorcycle. No specific delivery times, no regard for late night or early morning. The contents were always turning points in life: obituaries, sudden illnesses, acceptance notices, conscription orders. The moment they announced "Telegram!" at the door, the recipient's expression would change. It was a job that carried the weight of news every day.
tools: readiness for the weight of the news

timeline.text: Widespread telephone ownership shifts urgent communication to phones
Mobile phones and email make instant communication commonplace
Only ceremonial use for congratulatory and condolence telegrams remains

132.timelineClose: The role of "delivering as quickly as possible" was taken over by communication technology. But the demand for "formal messages that remain in physical form" survived, and congratulatory and condolence telegrams are still delivered today.
132.trivia: In the past, a late-night telegram was synonymous with bad news, and families would freeze at the sound of the doorbell. The fear brought by speed changes form but persists as communication gets faster—today, late-night smartphone notifications have taken on that role.
132.lineageText: Express messenger → Telegrapher → Telegram delivery → Telephone → SMS / Email

133.summary: A mountain occupation that involved catching pit vipers for medicinal purposes. It disappeared along with the market for folk remedies.
body: They would search for pit vipers in mountains and fields, catching them with specialized tools or bare hands and placing them in bags. The caught vipers were sold to pharmacies or dealers and processed into tonics and nutritional supplements. As a bite could be life-threatening, they needed to know the snakes' habits intimately and anticipate their movements. Many also caught them as a side job during the off-season for farming.

timeline.text: Institutionalization of pharmaceuticals changes the status of folk remedies
Widespread adoption of scientifically proven medicines
Disappears with the shrinking demand for folk remedies

133.timelineClose: What was "believed to be effective" was replaced by what was "proven to be effective." Like the Leech collector (NO.019), this was a disappearance due to advances in medicine.
133.trivia: Viper sake and viper powder still circulate in some areas as folk remedies for invigoration. Even if the professional catcher has disappeared, the demand, almost akin to a belief, has not completely vanished.
133.lineageText: Leech collector → Snake catcher → Pharmaceutical industry

134.summary: Peddlers who carried large loads of vegetables and fish, transported them to cities by train, and sold them door-to-door. Also known as "katsugi-ya" (carriers), this trade directly connected producers and consumers.
body: They would procure goods from farming or fishing villages, pack them into furoshiki cloths or carrying baskets, and head to the city on the first train. They would visit their regular customers' homes, sell everything that day, and return. Some lines even had dedicated "peddler trains." It was a business of physical strength and trust, commuting daily with heavy loads on their backs.

timeline.text: Supermarkets become the everyday shopping destination
Private cars and refrigerators enable bulk buying
Demand for peddlers disappears, and peddler trains are abolished

134.timelineClose: The business of "sellers bringing goods to customers' homes" changed to "customers going to stores." But online retail and home delivery are once again reversing that trend—the spirit of peddling is being revived in a new form.
134.trivia: The "peddler trains," with dedicated cars, were packed with carrying women. The memory of how they supported urban dinner tables is passed down along with the history of the railway lines.
134.lineageText: Street vendor → Traveling peddler → Supermarket → Online retail

135.summary: A keeper who watched over the town from atop a watchtower and rang a bell upon discovering a fire. Reporting infrastructure replaced human eyesight.
body: They would climb a tall tower in town and scan in all directions for smoke or flames. If a fire was spotted, they would ring a bell, using different patterns (rapid strikes for nearby fires, spaced strikes for distant ones) to inform the entire town of the location and scale. There were overnight shifts, requiring hours of vigilance in the cold wind. It was a job that served as the eyes of the entire town.

timeline.text: Telephone普及 shifts to "whoever spots it reports it"
Fire radio and fire alarms are established
Watchmen in towers become unnecessary

135.timelineClose: It's faster for everyone to report than for one person to watch. From centralized to decentralized surveillance—this structural shift eliminated the role of the watchman.
135.trivia: Fire watchtowers themselves still remain in various places, serving as local symbols and cultural assets. Even though the watchmen are gone, their workplaces continue to stand as part of the landscape.
135.lineageText: Fire watchtower keeper → Telephone reporting → Fire alarm / 119 emergency number

136.summary: Skilled professionals who executed trades by sending hand signals on the floor of stock exchanges. This occupation has a clear "death date": the closing day of the trading floor in 1999.
body: Floor traders were dispatched by securities firms to the trading floor, where they communicated orders using hand signals. Arbitrageurs matched these buy and sell orders to determine prices. Finger shapes and hand heights indicated stock, price, and quantity, allowing trades to be executed instantly amidst shouts. It was a physical, human trading system that used the entire body.
tools: the energy of the trading floor

timeline.text: Systematization of stock trading progresses
Tokyo Stock Exchange trading floor closes
Trading moves entirely into computers

136.timelineClose: On the closing day, applause reportedly erupted on the trading floor. The market created by human hand signals became, from that day forward, an event within servers. It is a rare profession whose death date is known to the minute.
136.trivia: Hand signals were a unique language, using finger shapes and positions to represent numbers. Skilled traders could accurately communicate with distant counterparts even amidst the noise. It was not electrical signals, but the shape of fingers, that moved the market.
136.lineageText: Floor trader → Electronic trading → Algorithmic trading

137.quote: i typed on a special machine
137.summary: A specialist who created documents using dedicated word processors. Lasting about 25 years from its birth to the end of production, it was one of the shortest-lived occupations.
body: Operating dedicated word processors, they created corporate documents, reports, and invitations. As operations varied by model and Japanese input conversion had its quirks, mastering the machine itself was a skill. There was a 'Word Processor Proficiency Test,' and companies employed dedicated operators who handled all document creation.

timeline.text: Japanese dedicated word processors first appear*
Personal computers become ubiquitous, diminishing the need for dedicated machines
Manufacturers cease production of dedicated word processors

137.timelineClose: Born as the next generation after typists (NO.097), they were overtaken by the subsequent generation (PCs) within a single generation. The pace of technological change was so rapid that the profession had no time to mature.
137.trivia: The 'Word processor operator' was removed from the census occupational classification. *From its appearance in statistics to its disappearance, it lasted one generation—a profession born and died within public records.
137.lineageText: Calculator operator → Keypunch operator → Typist → Word processor operator → PC → LLM

138.quote: i'll come collect every month, okay?
138.summary: A collector who visited homes and shops monthly to collect cash. The digitization of payments brought an end to these house calls.
body: They would visit policyholders in their assigned district each month, collecting insurance premiums and savings in cash, and recording them in passbooks or collection cards. Visiting the same homes on fixed days, they became familiar faces, engaging in small talk and even learning about family matters. Alongside collections, they also handled sales for new contracts.

timeline.text: Direct deposit and automatic bank transfers become widespread
The inefficiency and danger of cash collection become a concern
Removed from census occupational classification

138.timelineClose: Money shifted from 'hand-to-hand' to 'automatic withdrawal.' Behind this efficiency, the human connection of a stranger visiting homes every month also vanished.
138.trivia: Collectors also served as community guardians, sometimes noticing changes in elderly people living alone. The efficiency of payments stripped away the incidental social connections that came with the job.
138.lineageText: Collector → Automatic bank transfer → Cashless payment

139.summary: A brokerage business that traded 'telephone subscription rights' as assets. The rights themselves became worthless and disappeared.
body: The 'telephone subscription right' (facility installation charge), necessary to install a landline, was once an asset worth tens of thousands of yen. Brokers mediated between those who wished to sell and those who wished to buy these rights, earning a commission. They could be inherited, seized, or used as collateral. It was a unique financial business from an era when telephones were a luxury.
tools: Market price list for subscription rights

timeline.text: The spread of mobile phones reduces the necessity of landlines
The advent of IP phones and reduction in subscription fees cause asset value to plummet
Removed from occupational classification

139.timelineClose: It wasn't the product itself that disappeared, but its 'value.' When there's no longer a point in trading, the brokerage job also vanishes—an extinction where the entire market evaporated.
139.trivia: Telephone subscription rights were once considered property subject to inheritance tax and part of household assets. Today, the very idea of 'paying money to buy a right to install a phone' is incomprehensible to younger generations.
139.lineageText: Telephone rights broker → Mobile phones / IP phones

140.quote: i can spot a good cow
140.summary: An expert who brokered the buying and selling of cattle and horses for farming. A descendant of the 'Hakuraku,' their expertise became obsolete as livestock disappeared from agriculture.
body: They mediated the sale or purchase of cattle and horses for farmers. They judged age by teeth, strength by legs, and temperament by eyes. Livestock was a farmer's greatest asset, and judging their quality could make or break a business. They traveled between markets, setting prices between sellers and buyers—a merchant with an eye for living creatures.

timeline.text: Tillers and tractors replace draft animals
Cattle and horses disappear from farms
Removed from occupational classification

140.timelineClose: When machines drove out cattle and horses, the job of assessing them was also driven out. The profession of brokerage is doomed when the object of mediation disappears.
140.trivia: The term 'Hakuraku' originates from a Chinese legend referring to a master who could discern fine horses, and in Japan, it came to mean a livestock broker or healer. The skill of 'an eye for horses,' which lasted for thousands of years, vanished within decades due to the spread of tractors.

141.summary: A variety performer who used different celebrity voices, connecting the stage with song, dance, and storytelling. Though gone from statistics, the art form reincarnated on television and the internet.
body: They stood on stage, imitating the voices of popular actors and politicians of the time for laughs. A jack-of-all-trades performing song, dance, instruments, and storytelling alone, they toured vaudeville theaters, playhouses, and cabarets. Before television, when opportunities to hear celebrity voices were limited, vocal impressions were a precious form of 'mimicry' entertainment.

timeline.text: Television becomes the center of entertainment, reducing venues for stage variety acts
Specialization in entertainment eliminates the 'jack-of-all-trades performer' category
Removed from census occupational classification

141.timelineClose: Though they disappeared from classifications, they live on as 'impressionists' and 'variety show talents.' The disappearance from statistics is not the same as the disappearance of a culture—this card reminds us of that.
141.trivia: Before television, means of knowing celebrity voices were limited, so an impressionist's 'likeness' was partly completed by the audience's imagination. In an era where the real thing can be seen anytime, the very meaning of mimicry has changed.

142.summary: One of the most common jobs in the world: scanning product barcodes and receiving payment. Now, self-checkout and unmanned stores are quietly reducing their numbers.
body: They scan products, announce totals, accept cash or cards, and even handle bagging and age verification. What seems like simple work is actually the frontline of a store, dealing with complaints, making discount decisions, and ensuring security. Employing tens of millions worldwide, it is one of humanity's largest occupations.

The cash register machine itself was invented in 1879 by an American saloon owner to prevent employees from skimming sales. For 150 years since, the machine has continued to evolve, finally beginning to eliminate the human operator.

timeline.text: Self-checkout begins to spread
Cashier-less store 'Amazon Go' opens
The rest of this card has yet to be written

142.timelineClose: A larger reenactment of the trend that eliminated gas station attendants (NO.114) through self-service in Japan is underway. However, whether it will be complete extinction or a transformation into a customer service specialist role is yet to be decided.
142.trivia: When first invented, the cash register was called the 'incorruptible cashier,' a machine for owners to monitor employees. The machine designed to watch employees is now, 150 years later, attempting to replace the employees themselves.
142.lineageText: Street vendor → Peddler → Gas station attendant → Cashier → Self-checkout / Unmanned store

143.summary: They stood in toll booths, collecting tolls and giving change. With the spread of ETC, this is one of the fastest examples of a 'work in progress' reaching near 'completion.'
body: Standing in toll booths, they received tickets and cash from stopped cars, calculated the fee, and provided change and a receipt. Speed was essential, processing transactions in seconds to avoid delaying subsequent vehicles. Amidst exhaust fumes and noise, they worked 24-hour shifts, standing in their booths regardless of weather, at the forefront of traffic jams.
tools: Processing speed of a few seconds

timeline.text: ETC service begins in Japan*
ETC usage exceeds 90%, drastically reducing manned booths
The rest of this card has yet to be written

143.timelineClose: The technology that transformed 'stopping to pay' into 'passing without stopping' eliminated both the hassle of payment and the people who received it. Among these entries, it is the card closest to completion.
143.trivia: Before ETC, toll booths were always notorious for traffic jams. The technology introduced with the goal of 'eliminating congestion' incidentally led to the near-extinction of an entire profession. The purpose and outcome of technology often diverge.

144.summary: A job that continuously answered inquiries over the phone. A direct descendant of the telephone operator (NO.046), the same reason is now making its second visit.
body: Wearing a headset, they answered incoming calls one after another. Referring to manuals and systems, they processed orders, malfunctions, complaints, and cancellations. Response time, resolution rate, customer satisfaction—everything was managed by numbers. A prime example of emotional labor, it was common to be subjected to unreasonable anger.

timeline.text: Interactive Voice Response (IVR) and chatbots handle initial responses
Generative AI begins to enable natural conversational responses
The rest of this card has yet to be written

144.timelineClose: A hundred years ago, automatic exchanges eliminated telephone operators. Now, AI voice is coming to eliminate their descendants. Technology visits the same place in the same lineage twice.
144.trivia: Telephone operators (NO.046) were 'people who connected calls,' while call centers are 'people who answer calls.' Technology eliminated the former, and humans moved to the remaining 'part of talking to people.' And now, AI is poised to take over that last part too.
144.lineageText: Express messenger → Telegrapher → Telephone operator → Call center → AI voice bot

145.summary: A job solely focused on transcribing information from paper into digital format. They are the direct descendants of the Keypunch Operator (NO.057).
body: They would tirelessly type, looking at handwritten application forms, slips, and questionnaires. Accuracy was paramount, and a method called 'double punching' was often used, where two people would input the same data for verification. Speed and precision were everything, demanding the concentration to input thousands of entries in a single day.

timeline.text: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) accuracy reaches practical levels.
AI-OCR and RPA automate the reading of even handwritten documents.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

145.timelineClose: Calculator (NO.015) → Keypunch Operator (NO.057) → Typist (NO.097) → Data Entry Clerk. The job of 'humans passing information to machines' has followed the same fate, merely changing its method of delivery.
145.trivia: This job was originally born to 'have humans read what machines couldn't, and then pass it to the machines.' Once machines became capable of reading on their own, the fundamental reason for this profession's existence vanished. The reason for its beginning was also the reason for its end.
145.lineageText: Calculator → Keypunch Operator → Typist → Data Entry Clerk → AI-OCR・LLM

146.quote: i'm here to read the meter
146.summary: A visiting profession that involved going around to read electricity, gas, and water meters. They are quietly disappearing, unnoticed by most.
body: They would visit each house in their assigned district, read the meter values, and input them into a handheld device. Inside gates, under floors, in backyards—meters were in different locations for each house, and they would be barked at by dogs and walk even on rainy days. Beyond just reading numbers, they sometimes discovered gas leaks or abnormalities, and even noticed changes in elderly residents.

timeline.text: Installation of smart meters progresses.
Remote meter reading automatically transmits values, eliminating the need for visits.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

146.timelineClose: Once meters can transmit their own readings, there's no need for someone to go and read them. This is one of the professions disappearing most quietly, most unnoticed.
146.trivia: Meter readers were one of the few 'people who visited every house in a community' each month. With the disappearance of Bill Collectors (NO.138) and now meter readers, there will be almost no strangers left who regularly visit homes.
146.lineageText: Bill Collector → Meter Reader → Smart Meter

147.summary: The face of the bank, handling deposits, withdrawals, and procedures from behind the counter. As branch networks shrink, the very act of 'going to the bank' is fading away.
body: They would call customers by their number, receive passbooks and slips, and process deposits, withdrawals, transfers, account openings, and various other procedures. They counted cash, verified seals, and identified any deficiencies in documents. As a job dealing with trust, thorough accuracy and verification were demanded. Local branches also served as a window to daily life for the community.

timeline.text: The spread of ATMs moves routine deposits and withdrawals away from the counter.
Online banking and apps shift procedures to the screen.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

147.timelineClose: ATMs took over cash, and apps took over procedures. What remains is only consultation work, which is also decreasing in number with the consolidation and closure of branches.
147.trivia: Once, on payday, long queues formed at bank counters. Salary transfers, ATMs, and then cashless payments gradually dismantled those queues—the disappearance of the queues was a harbinger of the disappearance of the profession.

148.summary: Translators who specialized in manuals and routine documents. Rather than disappearing, they are transforming into 'AI proofreaders'—perhaps a re-enactment of the benshi → voice actor transition.
body: They would translate manuals, contracts, specifications, news articles, and more into other languages. This involved standardizing technical terms, adjusting for cultural differences, and resolving ambiguities in the original text—simply replacing words wouldn't suffice. It was a painstaking process of creating glossaries, accumulating past translations, and maintaining consistent quality.
tools: Ability to discern the original text's intent

timeline.text: Neural machine translation reaches practical levels.
Generative AI rapidly produces context-aware translations.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

148.timelineClose: The job isn't disappearing, but its position is shifting. From 'the person who translates' to 'the person who corrects AI translations (post-editor).' Just as the Benshi (NO.110) became a voice actor, the place for this skill is currently in transition.
148.trivia: Benshi lost their jobs with the advent of talkies, but many transitioned into voice actors and narrators. Technology often takes away only a part of a job, and people move into the remaining parts—that's what distinguishes transformation (◇) from disappearance (◆). Whether this card will be a transformation or a disappearance is yet to be decided.
148.lineageText: Nagasaki Interpreter → Translator → Machine Translation → Post-editing

149.summary: One of the largest professions of the modern era, transporting people and goods. This is the current point in the lineage of transportation: Horseman → Coachman → Driver → Autonomous Driving.
body: They transport passengers or cargo, driving on roads to reach destinations. Traffic jams, weather, sudden darting pedestrians, long hours of concentration—this is a comprehensive role that includes not just driving, but also handling cargo, customer service, and route judgment. They handle the 'last mile' of logistics, becoming the very infrastructure of society.

timeline.text: Development competition for autonomous driving technology intensifies.
Commercial operation of driverless taxis begins in some regions.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

149.timelineClose: Palanquin Bearers (NO.064) were replaced by rickshaws, and Hackney Coachmen (NO.030) by automobiles. On the same lineage, the very 'person who drives' is now being questioned. However, if loading/unloading and customer service are included, the replacement is not so simple.
149.trivia: Throughout this lineage, the bearer has always been 'the person who transports.' They survived by changing how they used their bodies: carrying → pulling → operating. Will they remain in another form even with autonomous driving—that is the question this card poses.
149.lineageText: Palanquin Bearer → Horseman → Hackney Coachman → Rickshaw Puller → Driver → Autonomous Driving

150.summary: An administrative role that involved keeping ledgers and reconciling numbers. They are descendants of the Calculator (NO.015), and ledgers are increasingly moving beyond human hands.
body: They would categorize receipts and invoices, record them in ledgers, and close the books monthly. If even one yen didn't match, they would trace back to find the cause. All-nighters were not uncommon during closing periods. While their job was to reconcile numbers, it was also an administrative role close to management, where they developed an eye for understanding a company's reality through its figures.
tools: Tenacity to track down every single yen

timeline.text: Cloud accounting begins to automatically import bank statements.
AI automatically categorizes journal entries, and OCR reads supporting documents.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

150.timelineClose: The 'recording' and 'reconciling' parts are becoming increasingly automated. Just as Calculators ceded calculations to machines, bookkeeping is also being ceded. Perhaps only the part of reading numbers and making judgments will remain.
150.trivia: Just as many Calculators (NO.015) became early programmers, people with bookkeeping knowledge are now moving into the design and operation of accounting systems. Often, the people who create machines that take over jobs are those who know those jobs best.
150.lineageText: Calculator → Bookkeeper → Accounting Software・Automated Journal Entry AI

151.summary: A shop that carves a person's name into a single stick of wood or horn, to be pressed in vermilion ink. The trade was held up by a paperwork custom unique to Japan — and it is the paperwork, not the tool, that is disappearing first.
body: A requested name is carved in mirror image into boxwood, water-buffalo horn, or — these days — resin. A registered seal is valuable precisely because no two are alike, so after a machine roughs out the characters, a blade is taken to each one by hand to break the symmetry. Rows of blanks lined the shopfront, alongside vermilion ink pads, stamping mats and seal cases.

Entering school, starting a job, marrying, buying a house — at every turning point in a life, people visited the seal shop. Prices ran from a cheap ready-made stamp to a formal registered seal, and that range was, in effect, the range of how heavy the paperwork was.
tools: Brush for laying out the characters
Vermilion ink pad and stamping mat

timeline.text: A government proclamation makes the registered seal an official institution, and seal shops spread nationwide.*
Government paperwork begins dropping the seal requirement, and contracts move to electronic signatures.
The rest of this card has yet to be written.

151.timelineClose: Nothing broke, and no carving skill was lost. What became unnecessary was the act of stamping itself. A job whose institution disappears before its tools does is rarer in this archive than you might expect.
151.trivia: The custom of stamping documents survives in Japan and only a handful of other places; most of the world has always signed instead. This trade is not so much losing to a new technology as standing at the end of a local convention that only Japan kept up.
151.lineageText: Kao signature → Seal shop → Digital seal → Electronic signature

001.quote: i'm the only one who can write
001.summary: In an era when the ability to read and write was itself a specialized skill possessed by only a handful, contracts, taxes, and prayers alike were all recorded by the hands of scribes.
body: In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, scribes were an elite profession, trained over several years in specialized schools. They inscribed tax records, royal decrees, and prayers to the gods onto papyrus or clay tablets. In societies where only a tiny fraction of the population could read and write, all information converged upon those who mastered the written word.

Even in medieval Europe, having letters and contracts written by a proxy was commonplace. From street-corner scriveners to royal secretaries, an era spanning millennia saw people make a living simply by being able to 'write.'

timeline.text: The invention of the printing press mechanizes document reproduction
Public education raises literacy rates, making 'writing' no longer a special skill
The role dissolves into office work, word processing, and voice input

001.timelineClose: Rather than vanishing, the scribe's role was distributed among all humanity. A society where everyone can write is, in other words, a society where everyone is a scribe.
001.trivia: In ancient Egypt, textbooks actually existed that exhorted students to 'become a scribe, for all other jobs are arduous,' listing the miseries of various professions. For thousands of years, it was a stable career parents recommended to their children.
001.lineageText: Scribe → Stenographer → Typist → Voice Recognition AI

002.quote: i carry the news in song
002.summary: In an age without books or radio, stories, music, and news traveled carried by wandering humans. Minstrels transported thousands of lines of narrative with only their memory and their voice.
body: In courts, markets, and roadside inns, they would play their harps or fiddles, singing epic tales and love songs. Their entire repertoire was memorized; a long epic poem could take an entire night. As they traveled from land to land, they also served as a news medium, carrying rumors and events from other towns.
Some found patrons and were retained by courts, while others continued their wandering. They were both 'distributors' and 'storage devices' for stories.

timeline.text: Printed books begin to reproduce stories on paper
Rising literacy rates cause 'reading entertainment' to surpass 'listening entertainment'
Records and radio replace the journey of song with airwaves

002.timelineClose: The work of carrying stories has not vanished. From enka singers selling songbooks, to wandering musicians performing in bars, and even today's streamers—it continues, simply changing its vessel.
002.trivia: Homer's *Iliad* and *Odyssey* were both sung and passed down by minstrels through memorization before they were ever written down. The wellspring of world literature lay within the memory of this vanished profession.
002.lineageText: Minstrel → Town Crier → Kawaraban Seller → Benshi (Silent Film Narrator) → Kamishibai Storyteller → Streamer

003.quote: i decorated each book by hand
003.summary: Before the birth of the printing press, books were copied by hand, one by one. It was this artisan who adorned their margins and initial letters with gold leaf and vibrant colors.
body: In monastic scriptoria or urban workshops, they would apply pigments and gold leaf to parchment pages. Chapter initials were rendered in the shapes of plants or animals, while margins might feature angels, monsters, or even playful, doodle-like drawings. Completing a single book could take months to several years.
In an era when books were treasures, illumination also served as a declaration: 'This book possesses such value.'

timeline.text: Gutenberg's printing press begins mass reproduction of books
Orders for handwritten manuscripts drastically decline, and workshops close
The art of decoration shifts to engraved illustrations, its spirit to book design

003.timelineClose: The moment 'making each book by hand' ceased to be a fundamental premise, the work of adorning those books also lost its foundation. They were among the first creators to be defeated by mechanical reproduction.
003.trivia: Some surviving medieval manuscripts still bear the paw prints of cats that walked across the pages, or the hurried excuses of scribes who spilled ink. Bugs from the era of manual labor were preserved for centuries, unable to be erased.
003.lineageText: Illuminator → Compositor → Linotype Operator → DTP (Desktop Publishing) → Generative AI Layout

004.summary: A profession whose very goals—transforming base metals into gold and creating elixirs of immortality—were ultimately disproven by science. Yet, its experimental tools and techniques survived, evolving into chemistry.
body: Securing patrons among royalty and nobility, they secluded themselves in workshops filled with furnaces and flasks. They melted metals, distilled liquids, altered compounds, and meticulously recorded their findings. Their ultimate goal was the 'Philosopher's Stone.' It was a high-risk court-appointed research position, with banishment or imprisonment awaiting those who failed to produce results.
To protect their secrets, records were written in codes and allegorical drawings. The monopolization of knowledge was their trade tool.

timeline.text: Modern science, emphasizing experimentation and verification, begins to emerge
Chemistry advances the understanding of elements, confirming that 'gold cannot be made'
Only the apparatus and techniques of alchemy remain in chemistry laboratories

004.timelineClose: The entire theoretical premise was fundamentally flawed. However, the daily practice of 'mixing, heating, and recording' was directly inherited by chemists.
004.trivia: Isaac Newton, discoverer of universal gravitation, dedicated as much, if not more, passion to the study of alchemy as he did to physics. His surviving manuscripts include extensive alchemical notebooks. Even for a genius, it was 'still science' at the time.

005.summary: A specialist physician hired by cities afflicted by the Black Death. Their bizarre appearance, with a beak-shaped mask stuffed with aromatic herbs, was a product of the mistaken theory that 'bad air carries disease.'
body: Contracted by cities, they would visit only plague patients. As contemporary medicine believed 'miasma' (bad air) caused disease, they filled their beak masks with herbs and spices and covered their entire bodies with long, waxed coats. To avoid direct contact with patients, examinations were conducted with a long stick.
Effective treatments were virtually non-existent, and much of their actual work involved recording death tolls and witnessing wills. They were also statisticians of death.

timeline.text: The beak costume becomes established, but fails to prevent the plague itself
Major epidemics subside, reducing demand for contracted physicians
The discovery of bacteria disproves the miasma theory, rendering the costume obsolete

005.timelineClose: Even if the theory was wrong, the idea of protective clothing itself was correct. The protective gear of modern infectious disease specialists is a distant descendant of this beak.
005.trivia: The beak mask is said to have been devised by Charles de L'Orme, a 17th-century French royal physician. Remaining as a symbol of terror, this image is now a popular costume for Halloween and the Venice Carnival.
005.lineageText: Plague Doctor → Barber-Surgeon → Modern Medicine → Diagnostic AI

006.quote: i cut hair, and teeth too
006.summary: Haircuts, tooth extractions, bloodletting, and even surgical incisions—all were performed by the same person in the same shop. Any work involving blades was bundled into a single profession.
body: In medieval Europe, physicians trained in academic medicine disdained procedures that soiled their hands. Thus, barbers, skilled in handling blades, took on tasks ranging from bloodletting and tooth extraction to lancing abscesses and even amputating limbs on the battlefield. Blood-stained bandages would be hung outside their shops to dry, serving as their very signboard.
Having teeth pulled at a barbershop—though crude by today's standards—was then a logical division of labor: 'entrust it to a professional with blades.'

timeline.text: Surgery begins to establish itself as an academic discipline
In Britain, the Company of Surgeons separates from the Company of Barbers
'Cutting for medicine' goes to surgeons, 'cutting for grooming' to barbers

006.timelineClose: A rare extinction where one profession underwent cellular division into two entirely distinct ones: doctor and barber. Both descendants remain active today.
006.trivia: The red and white stripes of a barber's pole are said to originate from the blood of bloodletting and bandages. That spinning striped pattern, seen in front of barbershops worldwide, is a direct remnant of a vanished profession's signboard.
006.lineageText: Plague Doctor → Barber-Surgeon → Modern Medicine → Diagnostic AI

007.quote: i even made the king laugh
007.summary: The only person permitted to mock the king in his presence. Using humor as a pretext, they served as a safety valve, delivering truths to the monarch that no one else dared to speak.
body: Serving the court in flamboyant attire and a cap adorned with bells, they entertained the king and his guests with songs, acrobatics, and wit. Their true work lay beyond this: using the pretense of 'a fool's words,' they conveyed criticisms or bad news to the king that his courtiers dared not utter.
A peculiar position, being at the heart of power yet outside its direct authority. It was a tightrope walk of humor, where displeasing the monarch could cost them their head.
tools: Discerning the limits of what could be said
