timeline.text: Court culture of absolute monarchy transforms, reducing the number of retained jesters
The role of satire shifts to newspapers and pamphlets
Critical humor is taken up by comedians and satirists

007.timelineClose: The court as a workplace vanished, but the function of 'laughing at power' itself remains indispensable to society, having relocated to the stage and media.
007.trivia: It is said that the worst news, such as defeat in battle, was deliberately conveyed by jesters. Even if the king raged at bad tidings, 'a fool's jest' was harder to punish—an unexpectedly rational design for organizational communication.

008.summary: Eating bread placed upon the chest of the deceased, they would take on that person's sins. This was a real-life subcontractor of souls, found in rural England.
body: Summoned when someone died in the village, they would eat the bread and drink the beer placed on the corpse, all while the family watched. This was a proxy service for a belief that the deceased's sins would transfer to the sin-eater, allowing the dead to journey lightly to the afterlife. Their payment was a meager sum of money.
As someone who accumulated sins, they were shunned by villagers and often lived on the outskirts of the community. It was a job that was both needed and simultaneously avoided.

timeline.text: The Church intensifies pressure, deeming this custom heretical
Modernization causes rural folk beliefs themselves to fade
The last known sin-eater passes away

008.timelineClose: With the evolution of religious views, the demand itself evaporated. It was a quiet end for a profession whose sole reason for existence was 'being believed in.'
008.trivia: The grave of Richard Munslow, the 'last sin-eater,' still exists in Shropshire, England, and has been restored by local residents. It is said that his main occupation was farming, and he took on sin-eating as a service to the village.
008.lineageText: Sin-eater → (No successor; vanished with the belief)

009.summary: At funerals, they would wail and weep on behalf of the bereaved. The profession of expressing grief as a proxy has existed worldwide since ancient times.
body: Upon request, they would join funeral processions and wakes, amplifying the sorrow of the occasion with their cries and lamentations. In societies where the volume and manner of weeping were believed to reflect the deceased's status, professional mourners were indispensable for a dignified funeral. Japan also had a similar occupation known as "nakibai" (weeping sellers) and others.
It wasn't just about crying; it was a skilled profession that involved singing improvised elegies woven with the life story of the deceased.

timeline.text: The funeral view of 'grief should be expressed quietly by family' spreads
Simplification and industrialization of funerals reduce demand for performance
Still active as a hired profession in some regions, such as East Asia

009.timelineClose: It hasn't completely vanished. The demand for emotional surrogacy can return as cultures change. This is a rare card where 'extinct' and 'active' coexist depending on the region.
009.trivia: Ancient Egyptian murals already depict processions of hired mourners. As far as records show, it can be considered one of humanity's oldest forms of emotional labor.

010.summary: A warrior class that dominated battlefields with armor, horses, and swords. The proliferation of firearms rendered both armor and chivalry obsolete, leaving only the title.
body: From childhood, they served as pages and squires, mastering martial arts and etiquette before being knighted. In wartime, they were the spearhead of heavy cavalry charges; in peacetime, they governed their lands and gained renown in jousting tournaments. Maintaining armor, warhorses, and retainers cost enormous sums, making it a profession heavily reliant on its equipment.

timeline.text: Longbows and dense infantry begin to undermine the dominance of heavy cavalry
Proliferation of firearms turns expensive armor into mere targets
Standing armies become the main force on the battlefield; knighthood becomes a title and ceremony

010.timelineClose: The moment their equipment became cost-prohibitive, they exited the battlefield as a social class. However, the title of 'Knight' continues to be bestowed in modern times.
010.trivia: The title 'Sir,' awarded to meritorious individuals in modern Britain, is a direct remnant of this profession. The sight of actors or scientists being knighted is, as it were, a live broadcast of a vanished profession becoming an honorary one.

011.summary: Legal pirates who received a commission from their government to attack enemy ships. A single international treaty rendered them illegal.
body: During wartime, they received a letter of marque from the government, authorizing them to attack and capture enemy merchant ships. The seized ships and cargo were sold after court review, and the proceeds distributed among the crew. The state could cheaply augment its naval power, while shipowners and sailors could aim for a fortune—it was a private contracting business for warfare.

timeline.text: Various nations utilize privateering as a naval strategy
Major powers agree to abolish privateering with the Declaration of Paris
State violence is consolidated under regular navies

011.timelineClose: It wasn't a decline in combat effectiveness, but a change in rules that outlawed the entire profession. This is one of the clearest examples of 'extinction by system'.
011.trivia: Sir Francis Drake, a hero of Elizabethan England, was seen by Spain as merely a pirate, but by England as a meritorious privateer knighted by the Queen. The line between legal and illegal was determined by the color of the flag.

012.summary: In an era before household taps, drinking water was something you bought. The job of carrying water in buckets or leather bags and selling it through city alleys existed worldwide.
body: They would draw water from rivers, wells, or springs, carry it in buckets on a shoulder pole or in leather bags on their backs, and sell it door-to-door. Knowing sources of good quality water was the lifeblood of their business; "that water carrier's water is delicious" was their very credibility. In Paris, Cairo, and Edo alike, their counterparts walked the alleys.

timeline.text: Modern cities begin laying public water systems
Pipes reach individual homes, and water changes from 'something to buy' to 'something to turn on'
The profession vanishes, and demand is absorbed by infrastructure

012.timelineClose: A water supply system is, in essence, the pipes that buried all the water carriers. It's the most classic pattern of infrastructure completely replacing a profession.
012.trivia: The modern sale of bottled water is, in a sense, a revival of the water carrier. However, it's no longer humans carrying it, but a logistics network.
012.lineageText: Water carrier → Public water supply → Bottled beverages

013.quote: please stay awake during the sermon
013.summary: An official in churches who would poke sleeping congregants with a long stick to wake them during sermons. It was the church version of a knocker-up.
body: During Sunday service, they would patrol the pews with a long stick. When they spotted someone nodding off, they would poke or gently tap them with the stick to wake them. In places where long, tedious sermons coincided with the weekly day of rest, drowsiness was the greatest enemy.
tools: Long stick with an ornamental tip

timeline.text: Forms of worship change, and sermons become shorter
Congregants are left to self-manage, and the position is no longer appointed
The battle against drowsiness becomes an individual responsibility

013.timelineClose: As the system relaxed, the position quietly vanished. A disappearance mourned by no one, yet it remains in the records.
013.trivia: It is said that the tips of the sticks were differentiated: a hard knob for waking men, and a feather or fox tail for women. *Even the method of waking had its etiquette.
013.lineageText: Sluggard-waker → Knocker-up → Alarm clock → Smartphone alarm

014.quote: i take care of everything for the king
014.summary: An attendant responsible for the King of England's personal needs, particularly during defecation, and one of the closest confidants in court. The one privy to the most private moments held the deepest secrets.
body: They attended to the King's personal care, especially during the most vulnerable times of excretion and dressing. Being present during the only moments the King was truly alone, they became privy to his true feelings and whispered confidences. Eventually, they were entrusted with managing the King's private purse, effectively becoming the chief confidant.
Far from being a dirty job, it was a coveted stepping stone for noble offspring vying for advancement.

timeline.text: Reaches the peak of its power during the reign of Henry VIII
Role is reduced and renamed with each court reform
The position disappears from the modernized royal household

014.timelineClose: When the King's private life was separated from the institutional system, official positions that intruded upon it became unnecessary. When the form of power changes, so too do the shortcuts to it.
014.trivia: The 'King's toilet attendant' was, in effect, the King's chief private secretary and financial advisor. Few historical positions have had such a disparity between their title and their actual function.
014.lineageText: Groom of the Stool → (Vanished with the modernization of court systems)

015.quote: they calculated everything by hand, you know
015.summary: Long before electronic computers, complex calculations were all done by human hands. 'Human Computers'—known in English as 'Computers'—were specialists who continuously created mathematical tables at observatories and research institutes.
body: In an era without electronic computers, observatories, military, and research institutes had 'computing rooms' where dozens of human computers sat at desks, constantly creating logarithm and ballistic tables. An answer produced by one person was always checked by another. They would repeat the process until both answers matched.

It was largely a workplace for women. The computing room at NACA, the predecessor to NASA, was called 'computers in skirts,' and their manual calculations became the foundation for the trajectories that would later carry humanity to the moon.

timeline.text: The electronic computer ENIAC appears
Electronic computers become widespread in research institutions
Computing rooms close. The name 'computer' remains only for the machines

015.timelineClose: Machines were faster and didn't make mistakes. Yet, it was the human computers who best understood the mechanisms of calculation, and many of them transitioned into early programmers. The first human programmers were the very people who yielded their work to machines.
015.trivia: Job advertisements read: 'Human Computers wanted. However, those who dislike calculation need not apply.' The film 'Hidden Figures' (2016) is a true story depicting the last generation of this profession.
015.lineageText: Human Computer → Keypuncher → Typist → Data entry ▲Currently vanishing

016.quote: i'll knock on your window until you wake up
016.summary: In an era when alarm clocks were still luxury items, there was a job of going around in the morning, knocking on clients' windows to wake them. In the industrial cities of Britain, a worker's day began with this sound.
body: They walked the dark streets before dawn, carrying a long bamboo pole. Upon reaching a client's house, they would gently tap on the second-story bedroom window. It was the professional's way not to leave until a reply was heard. If the window was too high, some would use a pea-shooter to fire peas at the window.

The fee was a contract of a few pence per week. They had to visit dozens of houses according to factory shifts, requiring them to memorize all routes and times. They would never knock on the windows of non-contracted houses, because if people woke up for free, it wouldn't be a business.

timeline.text: Alarm clocks begin to be mass-produced and their prices fall
Clocks become widespread in households with the spread of electricity
The last knocker-up retires

016.timelineClose: Human legs could never compete with cheap, accurate machines. Nevertheless, for over 100 years since the Industrial Revolution, this profession supported the mornings of Britain.
016.trivia: 'So, who wakes the knocker-up?'—This was a classic riddle of the time. The answer was 'no one wakes them.' This was because they were often night owls or workers finishing night shifts.
016.lineageText: Church Sluggard-waker → Knocker-up → Alarm clock → Smartphone alarm

017.quote: when evening comes, i light up the town
017.summary: In an era before electricity, streetlights were gas lamps. As dusk fell, lamplighters would ignite them one by one, and at dawn, extinguish them again, one by one. The nightscape of the city was crafted by this very profession.
body: As the sun set, they would shoulder a long pole called a 'lighting rod' and head to their assigned streets. The rod's tip held a small flame or a hook. Opening the gas lamp's valve and transferring the fire, the street would suddenly brighten. Dozens, sometimes over a hundred, lamps were lit each night.

The job wasn't over once the lamps were lit. Before dawn, they would walk the same route again, extinguishing each lamp one by one. During the day, they replaced gas mantles and cleaned the glass. Walking the same streets at the same time every night made them more intimately familiar with the city than anyone else.

timeline.text: Electric streetlights appear
Gas lamps are replaced by electric lights and become automated
Only a few ceremonial lamplighters remain active in London

017.timelineClose: In an age where a single switch illuminates an entire city, the reason for walking around to light each lamp individually vanished. However, the profession isn't entirely extinct. In London, approximately 1500 gas lamps are still in use today, maintained by just a handful of active lamplighters.
017.trivia: The lamplighter in 'The Little Prince' lives on a tiny planet where the sun sets every minute, endlessly lighting and extinguishing lamps as commanded. It is said that Saint-Exupéry chose this profession because it was 'the only adult who worked for something other than himself.'

018.summary: In cities without streetlights, these boys would carry torches, guiding pedestrians through the night. The moment the streets brightened, their profession dissolved into the darkness along with it.
body: They would wait for customers outside theaters and taverns, offering to guide them through the night for a few coppers. London's nights were truly dark, fraught with mud, uneven steps, and highwaymen. A single torch was the sole guarantee of safety and direction.
Some, it is said, even colluded with villains, deliberately leading customers into dark alleys. Those who held the light held dominion over the night.

timeline.text: Installation of gas lamps begins in cities
Main streets become illuminated at night, and the demand for guides disappears
Lighting becomes infrastructure, and the boys move to other street jobs

018.timelineClose: Each time a lamplighter illuminated a street, a link-boy's territory vanished. Employment simply shifted within the same 'work of light.'
018.trivia: On the gateposts of some old London mansions, conical metal fittings called 'link extinguishers' still remain, used by link-boys to put out their torches. Traces of the profession survive as architectural hardware.※

019.summary: In an era when 'bloodletting'—curing illnesses by having leeches suck blood—was common medical practice, there was a job for collecting these crucial leeches from swamps. The bait? Their own legs.
body: They would hike up their skirts, step barefoot into the swamp, and stand still. Eventually, leeches would attach themselves, and at the opportune moment, they would be peeled off and collected in a jar. While some used old horse legs, the most reliable bait was their own. It's said that collectors were often anemic from being bled all day.

The collected leeches were sold to apothecaries and doctors. The early 19th century saw an unprecedented leech craze in Europe, with France importing tens of millions annually. It was an age when leeches were prescribed for everything from headaches to fevers.

timeline.text: Overhunting drastically reduces leech populations, causing prices to skyrocket
Modern medicine begins to dispute the efficacy of bloodletting
Demand vanishes, and the profession sinks into oblivion

019.timelineClose: The very theory that 'removing bad blood would cure illness' was flawed. When the foundational doctrine collapses, the profession built upon it falls with it.
019.trivia: Leeches have quietly returned to the medical world. To prevent congestion in reattachment surgeries for severed fingers, for example, medicinal leeches were officially approved as 'medical devices' by the U.S. FDA in 2004.
019.lineageText: Plague Doctor → Barber Surgeon → Leech collector → Modern Medicine

020.summary: During the development of anatomy, medical schools faced a chronic shortage of cadavers. A black market emerged, digging up and selling 'educational materials' from cemeteries at night, only to be abolished by a single law.
body: They would dig up freshly buried graves at night and sell the bodies to medical schools. Using wooden shovels to avoid noise, they would only excavate the head-end, and after extracting the body, meticulously restore the site—their methods were professionally refined. A loophole in the law, which did not legally consider a corpse 'property,' meant that stealing one was difficult to prosecute as theft, thus sustaining the trade.

timeline.text: A case where the supply escalated to murder is exposed, igniting public outrage
The UK Anatomy Act is passed, establishing a legal system for cadaver supply
The black market disappears, and body donation systems take over

020.timelineClose: By redirecting demand to legal channels, the black market dried up overnight. This is an example of a profession eliminated not by prohibition, but by systemic design.
020.trivia: The Burke and Hare murders (1828), which triggered the change, represented the worst form of efficiency: the duo, finding digging too troublesome, began 'manufacturing' fresh cadavers themselves. The memory of the incident is etched into the name of the law.

021.summary: Small children were made to climb inside narrow chimneys to dislodge soot. This profession, driven by ethics into legislation, was gradually prohibited.
body: Boys, typically aged 4 to 10, bought as apprentices by masters, would climb bare-skinned from the fireplace into the chimney, scraping off soot with brushes, elbows, and knees. Their skin would be abraded, their lungs damaged by soot, and accidents where they became stuck in chimneys were frequent. It was a job where growing too large meant becoming 'unusable,' with growth itself being grounds for dismissal.

timeline.text: Movements exposing the reality and the invention of mechanical brushes advance
Following a fatal accident, climbing chimney sweeping is effectively banned in the UK※
Cleaning becomes a job for tools, and boys go to school

021.timelineClose: Technologically, it had long been replaceable. The continued use of cheap child labor was economic inertia; what stopped it was the law.
021.trivia: In British weddings, the custom of 'it's good luck to meet a chimney sweep' still persists, sometimes leading to a sweep (or someone in costume) being invited to the ceremony. The memory of a harsh profession lives on, transformed solely into a symbol of good fortune.
021.lineageText: Climbing boy → Mechanical brush → Child labor regulations

022.quote: they say you can tell by the shape of your head
022.summary: Experts in a 'science' that claimed to discern personality and talent from the bumps and indentations of the skull—a craze of the 19th century. The profession vanished when its theoretical foundation was entirely disproven.
body: They would palpate a client's head with both hands, diagnosing traits like 'cautiousness,' 'affection,' and 'combativeness' based on the location of cranial bumps. Their diagnoses were used as references for employment and marriage, phrenology parlors sprang up in entertainment districts, specialized magazines were published, and ceramic head models marked with zones sold like hotcakes.
It was the star service industry of its time, single-handedly performing what we now call personality assessments and aptitude tests.

timeline.text: Explodes in popularity in Europe and America, establishing itself as a profession
Advances in neuroscience scientifically disprove the theory
Exits both academia and the market

022.timelineClose: Only the idea of functional localization in the brain was carried forward by later science. Even with a wrong map, the intuition that 'there is a map in the brain' was correct.
022.trivia: White ceramic phrenology head models with marked zones are still sold worldwide as antique curios. The profession has vanished, but its diagnostic tools survive as interior decor.
022.lineageText: Phrenologist → Neuroscience (extinction due to theoretical disproval)

023.summary: In an era without refrigerators, ice was a natural resource harvested from winter lakes. This was a seasonal, arduous job of cutting ice blocks from frozen lake surfaces.
body: In the dead of winter, when lake ice reached sufficient thickness, it was time for 'ice harvesting' rather than fishing. Snow was cleared from the surface by horses, lines were drawn in a grid pattern, and large ice saws were used to manually cut out blocks. These ice blocks were floated through channels to the shore, then wrapped in sawdust and stored in ice houses. Keeping them from melting until summer was part of the skill.
By the 19th century, ice became an international commodity, and ice cutting supported a major industry.

timeline.text: Mechanical ice making (artificial ice) becomes practical
Loses market share, compounded by rumors that 'natural ice is unsanitary'
Ice transforms from something 'harvested' to something 'manufactured'

023.timelineClose: A natural resource dependent on weather lost to an industrial product available year-round. Today, natural ice survives as a niche delicacy, preserved by a few specialized shaved ice shops.
023.trivia: Frederick Tudor, America's 'Ice King,' amassed a fortune by exporting ice from Boston's lakes by ship all the way to Calcutta, India. Transporting a perishable commodity across the equator—it was the most audacious and successful logistics operation of the 19th century.
023.lineageText: Ice cutter → Iceman → Ice vendor → Electric refrigerator

024.quote: i deliver it before it melts
024.summary: In an era when refrigerators weren't yet electric, there was a job delivering blocks of ice by horse-drawn cart or truck to be placed in household 'iceboxes.'
body: In the morning, they would pick up giant ice blocks from the ice vendor's warehouse and tour their assigned city blocks. The signal for an order was an 'ICE card' posted in the window. The orientation of the card, marked with 25, 50, 75, or 100 pounds, indicated the amount of ice that household desired.

They would saw off the ordered amount, grasp it with ice tongs, hoist it onto their shoulder, and carry it to the kitchen icebox. In summer, it was a full day of hauling heavy ice and climbing stairs. Children would chase after the ice chips that fell from the cart—those were their summer treats.

timeline.text: Household electric refrigerators are invented
Refrigerator prices drop, and they begin to spread in urban areas
Iceboxes disappear, and delivery routes vanish along with them

024.timelineClose: The concept of 'coldness' shifted from something delivered to something produced in the kitchen. The iceman was a summer fixture in American cities, but ultimately lost to a single electrical outlet.
024.trivia: The same job existed in Japan (No. 106 Ice Vendor). With a wooden 'ice refrigerator' where ice was placed in the upper compartment and food below, ice vendors remained active until the 1960s (Showa 40s), when electric refrigerator penetration exceeded 90%.

025.summary: In an era when cities teemed with rats, there were specialists who hunted them with bare hands, ferrets, and dogs. Their skills have been passed down to modern pest control.
body: They took requests from grain warehouses, taverns, and sewers, releasing ferrets into burrows and catching the fleeing rats with terrier dogs and bare hands. While they used poisons and traps, their true skill lay in catching rats alive, as these could be sold to promoters of rat-baiting contests.
They were true professionals of the urban ecosystem, intimately familiar with the habits of rats.
tools: an eye for reading rat paths

timeline.text: Public health administration began to institutionalize pest control.
Chemical rodenticides and specialized companies replaced individual practitioners.
The profession continues as pest control.

025.timelineClose: What vanished was the style of the 'bare-handed hunter'—the demand itself has never disappeared. As long as there are cities, there will be rats.
025.trivia: Jack Black, a famous rat catcher who claimed to be employed by Queen Victoria, bred rats with unusual fur colors and sold them as pets to ladies. One origin of today's fancy rats as pets lies in the side business of pest controllers.

026.quote: hear ye, hear ye, news for you
026.summary: A 'human timeline' who rang a bell and loudly read out proclamations and news on the streets. They were the official broadcasters for citizens who couldn't read.
body: They gathered people with the cry of 'Oyez, Oyez (Hear ye!)' and a bell, then read out royal proclamations, tax notices, market announcements, and even news of lost children or incidents. In societies with low literacy rates, administrative information could only reach citizens through their voices. It was a public duty, and obstructing a town crier was considered a serious crime.
tools: formal attire and a tricorn hat

timeline.text: Newspapers began to handle information distribution in cities.
Rising literacy rates and improved postal services/bulletin boards reduced public duties.
A small number remain active in ceremonial and tourism roles in the UK and elsewhere.

026.timelineClose: The 'mass audio distribution' of information evolved into radio, and then into SNS notifications. The town crier's bell is now the vibration of a smartphone.
026.trivia: The cry 'Oyez' is Old French for 'Hear ye.' In the UK, national town crier competitions are still held, where participants compete in voice volume, clarity, and attire. It's an example of a profession preserved as a sport.
026.lineageText: Bard → Town crier → Kawaraban seller → Newspaper → SNS

027.summary: Children and elderly from impoverished communities who waited for low tide on the River Thames to scavenge coal, nails, and rope from the mud to sell. It has now been reborn as a licensed hobby.
body: When the tide receded, they would enter the muddy banks and search the mud with bare feet. They looked for fallen coal, copper nails detached from ships, rope fragments, and, if lucky, coins. What they found was sold to rag-and-bone men, providing money for the day's bread. It was a legitimate means of livelihood for London's lowest class.

timeline.text: Modernization of ports reduced 'spilled resources'.
Welfare and school education drew children away from the river.
Revived as a licensed hobby and archaeological activity with metal detectors.

027.timelineClose: A job born of poverty returned to the same muddy banks a century later as a hobby for a wealthy nation. Only what was scavenged changed, from bread money to historical artifacts.
027.trivia: Modern mudlarking requires an official license, and Roman coins and medieval rings are still found today. Discoveries must be reported to museums, meaning amateur finds contribute to archaeology.
027.lineageText: Mudlark → Tosher → Rag-and-bone man → Recycling industry

028.summary: An underground profession in London, diving into sewers to search for coins and metal washed downstream. Though dangerous, the earnings were good, making it an envied job in impoverished areas.
body: Armed with a lantern and a long pole, they entered the sewers, sifting through the mud for coins, spoons, and scrap metal. Gas, collapses, floods, swarms of rats—it was fraught with danger, but a good find could earn several times a day laborer's wage. Territory and empirical knowledge were their lifelines, and it was often a family trade, with skills passed from parent to child.
tools: a mental map of the sewers

timeline.text: Unauthorized entry was prohibited, and enforcement intensified.
Modernization and sealing of sewers made physical entry impossible.
The underground scavenging economy disappeared.

028.timelineClose: The modernization of infrastructure closed off not just the gaps in the infrastructure, but also the professions that thrived within them. There is no longer an economy of lost items within sealed pipes.
028.trivia: Toshers were practically masters of the sewers, and detailed testimonies remain in journalist Henry Mayhew's investigations into the poor of the time. London's underground economy can still be read about after its disappearance, thanks to journalism.
028.lineageText: Mudlark → Tosher → Rag-and-bone man → Recycling industry

029.summary: A urban recycling profession that went around with a pushcart or horse-drawn cart, calling out 'Rags, bones, scrap metal~' and buying unwanted household items. They are in the same lineage as Japan's 'kuzuya' (junk dealers).
body: Rags became raw material for paper, bones for fertilizer, buttons, or glue, and metal for remelting—everything collected could be sold to merchants. In an era when waste was still a resource, this job drove the final stage of urban material circulation. Their bells and distinctive cries were signals to the neighborhood.

timeline.text: Mass production and consumption reduced the resource value of rags.
Municipal waste collection replaced individual practitioners.
Reborn within the system as the recycling industry.

029.timelineClose: The 'person who buys trash' disappeared, but the underlying principle was absorbed by public administration as resource collection. One could say that the horse-drawn cart simply transformed into a collection vehicle.
029.trivia: They bought bones because they could be crushed for fertilizer, boiled for glue, or carved into buttons. A zero-waste urban economy, in fact, was already established in the 19th century.
029.lineageText: Rag-and-bone man → Junk dealer → Waste collection → Recycling industry

030.summary: The direct ancestor of taxi drivers, who transported passengers in hackney carriages. The very word 'cab' transitioned from horse-drawn to automobile.
body: They waited for passengers at street corners, then drove their carriages after hearing the destination. They memorized urban shortcuts and fare rates, and rainy days were prime earning opportunities. Caring for the horse and managing its temperament accounted for half the job, and a coachman's skill was judged by their handling of the horse. In London, Paris, and Tokyo (before the 'en-taku' taxi), this profession was the primary mode of urban transport.
tools: an eye for passengers and horses

timeline.text: Gasoline-powered taxis appeared.
Urban horse-drawn carriages rapidly transitioned to automobiles.
Many coachmen retrained as drivers.

030.timelineClose: The vehicle changed, but the core structure of the job—'picking up passengers at street corners and transporting them'—remained the same. Only the motive power, not the essence of the profession, died.
030.trivia: The word 'cab' is an abbreviation of 'cabriolet,' a type of carriage, and the legal official name for taxis in London is still 'Hackney Carriage.' On paper, the era of the coachman has not yet ended.
030.lineageText: Palanquin bearer → Coachman / Cabman → Rickshaw puller → Driver → Autonomous driving

031.summary: In the era when horses were the main mode of transport, they were the 'horse shoemakers' responsible for making and fitting horseshoes, and caring for hooves. They survive in the world of horse racing and riding.
body: They heated iron in a forge, hammered out a horseshoe to fit the horse's hoof, then trimmed the hoof and attached the shoe with nails. Hooves were crucial to a horse's health, and farriers also played a role akin to an entry-level veterinarian, discerning lameness by observing the horse's gait. It was a skilled profession encompassing both blacksmithing and animal care.

timeline.text: Horses began to disappear from urban transport.
Demand drastically decreased as farm horses were replaced by tractors.
Survives as a specialist for racehorses and riding horses (certified farrier).

031.timelineClose: The profession shrank in proportion to the decline in the total number of horses, but it remains absolutely essential as long as horses exist. In Japan, it has been passed down through the certified farrier qualification system.
031.trivia: The Western superstition that 'a found horseshoe is a lucky charm' is said to be a remnant from an era when horseshoes were expensive iron products, and finding one genuinely brought good fortune (i.e., it could be exchanged for money).
031.lineageText: Farrier → Auto mechanic (survives as a certified farrier in the equine field)

032.summary: A specialized craftsman who made wooden wheels for carts and carriages. The 'wheel-making profession,' which lasted for thousands of years, became entirely obsolete with the advent of rubber tires.
body: They carved the hub, spokes, and rim from different types of wood, then assembled the wheel. A heated, expanded iron tire was fitted onto the outer circumference of the assembled wheel and rapidly cooled. The contracting force of the iron tightened the entire structure, integrating the wheel without nails—the moment of 'tire shrinking' was the craftsman's highlight.
tools: an eye for wood grain and warping

timeline.text: Pneumatic rubber tires were commercialized.
The spread of automobiles eliminated demand for wooden wheels.
Skills preserved in museums and cultural heritage restoration.

032.timelineClose: Wheels, in fact, continued to proliferate, but the reason for making them from wood simply vanished. It's a classic example of a change in material rendering a profession obsolete.
032.trivia: The English surname 'Wheelwright' is derived directly from the name of this profession. Similarly, the surnames 'Cartwright' and 'Cooper' also preserve vanished occupations.

033.quote: the wood's curve, a work of my paws
033.summary: Beer, salt, nails, gunpowder—the barrel was once the king of transport containers. This star artisan, who supported all logistics, survives today in the world of whiskey barrels.
body: Oak staves, heated and bent by fire, are bound with hoops to create barrels that hold water without a single leak. This highly skilled craft, requiring no adhesive and relying solely on the tension of the staves for a perfect seal, involved apprenticeships lasting several years. Cooperages were indispensable near port towns and breweries, and the barrel's standard size even became a unit of trade—the 'barrel'.

timeline.text: Metal cans and drums enter the transport container market
Cardboard and pallets become the mainstays of logistics
Continues to exist as a specialist in aging barrels for whiskey and wine

033.timelineClose: It became extinct as a 'transport container' but survived solely as a 'flavor-making device.' It is a transformed occupation, extending its life by shedding one of its roles.
033.trivia: The 'barrel' as a unit of oil trade is a direct legacy from the era when barrels reigned as the primary container. The unit of a cooper's work is still announced daily in global economic news.
033.lineageText: Cooper → Metal containers, Cardboard (survives as an aging barrel cooper)

034.quote: i weave it, one row at a time
034.summary: A core cottage industry before the Industrial Revolution, hand weavers earned their living by weaving cloth on looms at home. They became the first symbol of workers whose jobs were taken by machines.
body: Using hand looms set up in their homes, they wove custom cloth one row at a time. This was a family-wide cottage industry, often combined with farming, supplying local textile merchants. Skilled weavers commanded high wages, even enjoying the luxury of 'Holy Monday,' resting the first half of the week to focus on work later.

timeline.text: Power looms are invented, beginning factory-based weaving
The Luddite movement emerges, as weavers losing their jobs destroy machinery
Hand-weaving wages collapse, making it unsustainable as a profession

034.timelineClose: Only the name of the resistance movement, 'Luddite'—meaning 'opponent of technology'—remains in modern language. Its reappearance in the age of AI is no coincidence.
034.trivia: The Luddites issued manifestos in the name of their legendary leader, 'General Ludd,' who was a non-existent figure. Those defeated by machines could only fight by invoking a fictional leader.
034.lineageText: Hand weaver → Power loom → Textile factory

035.quote: under the machine is my spot
035.summary: Children who crawled under operating spinning machines to clean up lint and cotton dust. Their small stature was a condition of employment.
body: Giant spinning mules continuously moved back and forth, dropping lint onto the floor. Stopping the machines would reduce production, so children aged 8 to 13 would crawl underneath the moving machinery, sweeping up debris and scrambling out before the carriage returned. It was a race against time, where a misstep could mean being crushed.

timeline.text: British Factory Acts begin regulating child labor
Stricter regulations and machine improvements eliminate the need for 'crawling cleanup'
Children are moved from factories to schools

035.timelineClose: It was not technological progress, but society's ethics that first ended this profession. The law prohibited the calculation that 'children are cheaper than the cost of stopping the machines.'
035.trivia: Testimonies from the children themselves are preserved in the records of factory investigation committees from that era. For the labor of the voiceless to disappear, their voices first needed to be recorded in public documents.
035.lineageText: Mule scavenger → Factory safety regulations, Automated cleaning

036.quote: i separate the stones from the coal
036.summary: Child laborers who sorted stones from flowing coal by hand in coal mine breaker houses. A series of photographs brought an end to this occupation.
body: Straddling steep-sloped coal breakers, they picked slate and stones by hand from the coal flowing beneath their feet. Covered in black dust, their fingers were so abraded they were called 'red claws.' Entering around age 10, they would move into the mines as they grew—it was the gateway to a life in coal mining.

timeline.text: Photographer Lewis Hine documents the reality and publishes it nationwide
Public opinion shifts, leading to stronger state child labor laws
With the spread of mechanical coal sorting, boys disappear from breaker houses

036.timelineClose: It was not statistics or speeches, but photographs that moved public opinion. This stands in labor history as an early example of media ending an occupation.
036.trivia: Hine infiltrated factories under false pretenses, posing as an 'insurance investigator' and other roles to take his photographs. It was precisely because the act of documenting was so perilous for the photographer that the images proved stronger than laws.
036.lineageText: Breaker boy → Coal sorting machinery → Child labor regulations

037.summary: Women and girls who worked in yellow phosphorus match factories. They are known for the occupational disease that rotted their jawbones and for a historic strike.
body: On the production lines for matches using yellow (or white) phosphorus as the igniting agent, workers faced long hours and low wages. Furthermore, continuous inhalation of phosphorus vapor led to an epidemic of 'phossy jaw,' a necrosis of the jawbone. Safer red phosphorus matches already existed, but yellow phosphorus was cheaper.

timeline.text: Match girls in a London factory go on strike and win
Yellow phosphorus matches are progressively banned by international treaties and national laws
Production shifts to industrial manufacturing of safety matches

037.timelineClose: The poison, continuously used 'because it was cheap,' was finally stopped by the voices of those affected and by legislation. This strike marked a turning point in the history of labor movements.
037.trivia: The 1888 strike was led by teenage match girls, considered among the most vulnerable in society. The voices raised by these most marginalized workers resonated the loudest and left the deepest mark on history.
037.lineageText: Match girl → Industrial production of safety matches → Labor safety laws

038.summary: Railway maintenance workers in America who straightened tracks to the rhythm of their songs. Their work songs became one of the wellsprings of the blues.
body: When tracks shifted under the weight of trains, large groups would insert crowbars and, to the rhythm of shouts and songs, apply force in unison to realign them. Because the work wouldn't move without perfect coordination, a lead singer would improvise songs to synchronize everyone's timing. Song was a tool.

timeline.text: Mechanization of track maintenance progresses
Large track maintenance machines replace manual tamping
Work no longer required singing

038.timelineClose: Machines could fix the tracks, but they couldn't sing. The work songs that vanished with the job now only live on in recordings and the blues.
038.trivia: The origin of the name 'Gandy dancer' is debated, with theories including a tool manufacturer's name or the workers' movements resembling a dance; it remains unconfirmed. It is an occupation that vanished, taking the mystery of its name's origin with it.

039.summary: Riders of the express mail service who crossed the continent by relaying horses. With the advent of the telegraph, it vanished after only about 18 months of operation, making it one of the shortest-lived professions in history.
body: Covering approximately 3000 km from Missouri to California, they delivered mail in about 10 days, changing horses at each station and riders along the way. Riders were chosen for their light weight and youth, riding continuously through bad weather and night. Though the pay was high, there was no guarantee of life.

timeline.text: Service begins, becoming the fastest communication to the West
Transcontinental telegraph line is completed
Discontinuation announced two days after completion*

039.timelineClose: It literally ended the day the telegraph wires were laid. It is rare for a technological generational shift to cut off an occupation so distinctly by a 'date.'
039.trivia: The anecdote of a rider recruitment advertisement stating 'orphans preferred' is famous, but no actual advertisement has been confirmed, making it likely a later fabrication. Including its legends, this occupation became a myth of the American West.
039.lineageText: Pony Express rider → Telegraphist → Telephone → Email

040.summary: Professionals who spanned continents and oceans with Morse code. They were the progenitors of all long-distance communication professions.
body: They tapped a telegraph key to send signals and transcribed incoming sounds into text by ear. Skilled telegraphists could send and receive dozens of words per minute, even discerning 'who was tapping' by the unique rhythm of their keystrokes. Railways, news, finance—all industries where speed meant money depended on the fingertips of the telegraphist.

timeline.text: Telephones begin carrying voice itself
Telex and FAX replace commercial communication
Morse code no longer used in shipping or military, moves to hobbyist realm

040.timelineClose: Humans were no longer needed to mediate the signals. However, in the world of amateur radio, the fingers tapping the telegraph key are still very much alive.
040.trivia: Telegraphists even engaged in casual chats and romances over the lines during breaks. In 1879, the novel 'Wired Love,' depicting online romance among telegraphists, was published. The originators of online dating were, quite literally, on the wire.
040.lineageText: Hikyaku (Express messenger) → Telegraphist → Telephone operator → Call center → AI voice bot

041.summary: Boys in uniform who rode bicycles to deliver telegrams that arrived by telegraph. They handled the 'last mile' of urgent news delivery.
body: Stationed at the telegraph office, they would race off on their bicycles in uniform whenever a telegram arrived. Business deals, obituaries, draft notices—telegrams were synonymous with urgency, and a single knock at the door could change a family's fate. Tips were their main source of income, and speed and courtesy were their performance metrics.

timeline.text: Demand for 'urgent written news' began to decline with the spread of telephones.
Home telephones became common, and telegrams dwindled to ceremonial use.
The boys' bicycle messenger service was absorbed by postal services and telephones.

041.timelineClose: During wartime, it was also these boys' duty to deliver casualty notices. The fastest communication also delivered the heaviest news with the greatest speed.
041.trivia: The same job existed in Japan (NO.132 Telegram Messenger), and the late-night cry of 'Telegram!' is etched into a generation's memory as a signal of emergency. All over the world, boys in the same uniform pedaled up the same hills.
041.lineageText: Hikyaku (foot messenger) → Telegrapher → Telegram messenger boy → Telephone → SMS

042.quote: a job reading books to everyone
042.summary: A professional reader who read newspapers and novels aloud to workers in cigar factories. Their employer was not the company, but the laborers themselves.
body: Sitting on a raised chair in a factory where monotonous manual labor continued, they would read newspapers and political commentaries in the morning, and novels in the afternoon. Their salary was paid by the workers pooling their wages, and what to read was decided by vote. The reader's voice and education determined the quality of the workplace—they were a cultural wellspring.

timeline.text: Radios began to be brought into factories.
Management also began to move to exclude lectors, deeming them 'agitators'.
The voice in the workplace was replaced by speakers.

042.timelineClose: The intellect hired by the workers themselves, at their own expense, was defeated by mass broadcasting. Today, it is quietly being revived as a tradition in some factories in Cuba and Florida.
042.trivia: The luxury cigar brand 'Montecristo' was named after 'The Count of Monte Cristo,' a novel read aloud in factories and beloved by the workers. The voice of the lector is preserved within the brand name.

043.quote: don't move, just for a bit
043.summary: A photographer specializing in the daguerreotype, the world's first practical photographic process. They were overtaken by faster, cheaper next-generation technologies in just about 20 years.
body: They would sensitize a polished silver-plated copper sheet, expose it in a camera for several tens of seconds, then develop it with mercury vapor. Subjects had their heads supported by a brace, holding their breath and remaining still. Each plate was a unique, irreproducible item, housed in a small case and treated like a treasure.

timeline.text: The daguerreotype was publicly introduced, and the profession of photographer was born.
Reproducible and inexpensive wet collodion photography emerged.
Daguerreotypes were driven out of the market.

043.timelineClose: The first generation of photography was killed by the second generation of photography. It was a profession born of technology, and killed by technology in just one generation.
043.trivia: The reason all subjects in early portrait photographs have serious expressions is that it was impossible to hold a smile for the several tens of seconds of exposure. The cultural norm of 'serious faces in photos' is a fossil of technological constraints.
043.lineageText: Daguerreotypist → Photo studio → Photo developer → Digital photography

044.quote: i picked up each letter, one by one
044.summary: A core printing profession that involved picking up individual type characters and arranging them into lines of mirror-image text to create a printing plate. It marked the end of a job that had lasted 500 years since Gutenberg.
body: From a wall-sized type case, they would pick up individual type characters according to the manuscript and arrange them in a composing stick. All characters were mirror images, reversed left-to-right, and were read and set upside down. Japanese compositors memorized the shelf locations of thousands of kanji characters by heart. Speed and accuracy were direct measures of a craftsman's skill.
tools: Memory of thousands of character locations

timeline.text: Phototypesetting began to replace metal type.
With the advent of DTP, typesetting became a computer task.
Hot metal typesetting virtually disappeared from newspapers and publishing.

044.timelineClose: For a technology that lasted 500 years, its end was instantaneous. Along with the weight of the lead, movable type vanished from printing houses.
044.trivia: One theory suggests that the English idiom 'mind your p's and q's' (meaning 'be careful of your manners') originated from compositors easily confusing the mirror-image letters p and q (other theories exist). An occupational hazard survived as a proverb.
044.lineageText: Manuscript illuminator → Compositor → Linotype operator → Phototypesetting → DTP → Generative AI layout

045.summary: An operator of an automatic typesetting machine that cast 'entire lines' of type from molten lead. They were artisans of lead and steam, supporting the rapid news delivery system of newspapers.
body: Striking a unique 90-key keyboard would align matrices, into which molten lead alloy was poured to cast a full line of type. This allowed for mass typesetting of daily newspapers at many times the speed of manual composition. The machines were hot, the lead heavy, and the air in the workplace smelled of oil and metal.

timeline.text: Linotype machines spread to newspaper companies, overwhelming manual typesetting.
Transition to phototypesetting and offset printing began.
With the advent of DTP, operators, along with their machines, exited the stage.

045.timelineClose: The machine that killed manual typesetting was, a century later, killed by computerized phototypesetting. It was a magnificent intermediary in the technological food chain.
045.trivia: The sequence 'ETAOIN SHRDLU' on the left side of the keyboard was often printed as a typo on pages, used as throwaway characters to fill error lines, and became a catchphrase in the printing industry. A meaningless incantation remains as an epitaph for the profession.
045.lineageText: Compositor → Linotype operator → Phototypesetting → DTP → Generative AI layout

046.summary: Initially, you couldn't dial someone directly. You'd first connect to an operator, say 'to number XX,' and the operator would then plug in the cords to connect the line. Every single call had a human intermediary.
body: Before them was a switchboard full of holes. Wearing a headset, they would take requests and insert the plug at the end of a cord into the hole for the desired number, connecting the call. Skilled operators kept both hands constantly moving, managing multiple calls simultaneously.

In Japan, this job emerged in Meiji 23 (1890) with the opening of the Tokyo-Yokohama telephone line. It was a glamorous profession for young women, requiring precise speech and a good memory. Operators knew exactly who in town talked to whom—it was an era with little regard for privacy.

timeline.text: Automatic exchanges appeared, and dial telephones began to spread.
Automatic direct dialing was completed across Japan.
Operators transitioned to information desk staff, then to call centers.

046.timelineClose: Dialing a number meant a machine would connect you automatically. Technically, the need for human intervention had long disappeared. Yet, it took nearly 90 years from the initial opening for telephone services nationwide to become fully automated.
046.trivia: The world's first telephone operators were boys. However, they were foul-mouthed and mischievous, so telephone companies quickly switched to women. The reason the 'voice on the other end of the phone' became female was due to the boys' misconduct.
046.lineageText: Hikyaku (foot messenger) → Telegrapher → Switchboard operator → Call center ▲disappearing → AI voice bot

047.summary: In an era without automatic operation, elevators had dedicated attendants. They were customer service professionals who controlled ascent and descent with a lever, announced floors, and opened and closed doors.
body: They would adjust speed with a manual lever, stopping precisely so the floor of the car aligned perfectly with the destination floor. Since passengers could trip on any height difference, stopping accuracy was a mark of skill. They announced floors and departments, opened and closed doors, and managed crowds. In Japan, 'elevator girls' became the face of department stores.

timeline.text: Automatic control and push-button elevators became widespread.
Operators began to disappear from office buildings.
Elevator girls also disappeared due to staff reductions in department stores.

047.timelineClose: Against machines that stopped precisely with the push of a button, the added value of customer service alone could not prevail. The voice of 'going up!' was replaced by recordings and chimes.
047.trivia: In the early days of automatic elevator adoption, people were afraid to ride 'boxes without drivers.' To alleviate this, synthetic voice announcements for reassurance and the 'Close' button were introduced. The history of automation is also a history of ingenuity in soothing human anxieties.

048.quote: i arranged them all by hand
048.summary: Boys who worked at the back of bowling lanes, manually resetting fallen pins and returning balls. They disappeared with the advent of automatic machines.
body: Sitting in the pit at the back of the lane, they would dodge thrown balls and pins, collect fallen pins, and quickly reset them to their designated positions. Balls were rolled back down the lane by hand. It was a job requiring quickness, constantly risking being hit by pins. Many were boys working after school.

timeline.text: The automatic pinsetter machine was invented.
Automatic machines became widespread in bowling alleys across the U.S.
The sight of boys disappeared from the pit.

048.timelineClose: Machines don't tire, nor do they feel pain when hit by pins. Dangerous, repetitive tasks are the earliest targets for mechanization.
048.trivia: The spread of automatic pinsetters transformed bowling from a 'game requiring dangerous backstage labor' into 'casual entertainment for everyone,' sparking the post-war American bowling boom. With the disappearance of the backstage workers, the entertainment itself became democratized.

049.quote: i kept the light all by myself
049.summary: A guardian who lived in lighthouses on capes and remote islands, tending the light through the night. In Japan, the last manned lighthouse became automated in 2006, making this a profession whose 'date of demise' can be precisely identified.
body: They lit the lamp at sunset and extinguished it at dawn. They regularly wound the weights that rotated the lens, polished the glass, refilled the oil, and sounded the foghorn on misty nights. They recorded the weather and watched over passing ships. If the light went out for even one night, a ship might sink—for that sole reason, they lived with their families on remote capes.

Supply ships arrived only once every few weeks. Children either commuted to school from the lighthouse or, on inaccessible islands, were homeschooled by their parents. It was a profession where the boundaries between work and life simply did not exist.

timeline.text: Electrification and automatic flashing devices reduced the need for human operation of the light.
The spread of remote monitoring gradually automated lighthouses across the country.
With the automation of the Onnajima Lighthouse in Nagasaki, Japan's manned lighthouses became zero*.

049.timelineClose: Automation progressed little by little, and the day the last one ceased operation was recorded. While many professions vanish unnoticed, this one has a specific date.
049.trivia: The film 'Times of Joy and Sorrow' (1957), depicting a lighthouse keeper couple, became a huge hit with its story of a family moving from lighthouse to lighthouse across Japan. The Japanese image of a lighthouse keeper was thus preserved in a single film, half a century before the profession itself vanished.
049.lineageText: Fire watchtower guard → Lighthouse keeper → Automatic flashing / Remote monitoring

050.quote: i grew them with my blood
050.summary: A research profession that involved feeding lice with one's own blood to produce typhus vaccines. In occupied Poland, it also served as a cover to protect the lives of intellectuals.
body: To culture the pathogens of epidemic typhus, it was necessary to breed a large number of lice, which acted as vectors. Louse-feeders would strap small cages of lice to their thighs daily, allowing them to feed on their own blood. It was a literally self-sacrificing job, enduring both itching and the risk of infection.

timeline.text: Louse-feeders were essential for typhus vaccine research.
Vaccine production became industrialized and sterilized.
Human-based feeding became unnecessary.

050.timelineClose: Advances in medical technology eliminated one of the most arduous, human-dependent jobs. This is one of the rare instances where technological progress liberated workers from severe hardship.
050.trivia: At the Weigl Institute in Nazi-occupied Poland, the status of 'louse-feeder' provided protection from forced labor and deportation. Scholars and resistance fighters survived by allowing lice to feed on their blood.* A job that literally consumed life, paradoxically saved lives.
050.lineageText: Louse-feeder → Industrial production of typhus vaccine

051.summary: Young women who painted the glowing dials of clocks and instruments with radium paint. The tragedy of their exposure through licking their brushes led to the creation of worker protection laws.
body: They used fine brushes to apply luminous paint, drawing numbers on the dials of clocks and instruments. To achieve fine lines, factories instructed them to 'lip-point' their brushes by licking the tips. They were unaware that the radium in the paint was a radioactive substance. Some even played in the workshop, making their nails and teeth glow with the paint.

timeline.text: Demand for luminous dials increased in the military and watch industries.
The 'Radium Girls' successively succumbed to jaw necrosis and anemia.
Following lawsuits and public outcry, safety regulations and working conditions improved.

051.timelineClose: The lawsuits brought by the victims paved the way for holding companies accountable for workers' health. Their sacrifice became the foundation of modern labor safety standards.
051.trivia: The remains of the 'Radium Girls' still emit faint radiation, serving as valuable records for researchers studying the long-term effects of radiation exposure. Even after death, they continue to provide data for labor safety.
051.lineageText: Radium dial painter → Labor safety legislation

052.summary: Black men who served as attendants on America's luxurious Pullman sleeper trains. Despite harsh working conditions, it was a historic profession that fostered the Black middle class and the Civil Rights Movement.
body: They single-handedly managed bed setup, shoe shining, luggage handling, and passenger care. Enduring long hours, low wages, and reliance on tips, their dignity was often eroded by passengers uniformly calling them 'George.' Yet, the stable cash income was invaluable for Black men at the time. Traveling across the nation, they also served as carriers of information and newspapers to various communities.

timeline.text: A Black-led labor union won collective bargaining rights*.
Sleeper trains declined with the spread of automobiles and airplanes.
The profession shrank, and its roles shifted to flight attendants.

052.timelineClose: This profession, which produced numerous leaders for both the labor and civil rights movements, continued to impact society in the form of its human legacy even after it vanished.
052.trivia: Guides like the 'Green Book,' published by the Pullman porters' union, which listed safe establishments and accommodations for Black travelers, emerged from their nationwide network. A mobile profession created a map for freedom of movement.*

053.quote: your morning milk, fresh for you
053.summary: The regular delivery person who brought glass bottles of milk to doorsteps every morning. The profession nearly vanished with the spread of refrigerators but has partially revived as a subscription service.
body: Before dawn, they would drive through residential areas, leaving milk bottles at each doorstep and collecting the previous day's empties. For homes without refrigerators, daily fresh milk delivery was essential. The familiar milkman also served as a watchful eye over the community.

timeline.text: The spread of household refrigerators made 'daily delivery' unnecessary.
Bulk buying at supermarkets became mainstream.
Partially revived through home delivery subscriptions and specialty milk services.

053.timelineClose: The model of 'regular delivery to the doorstep' itself never truly died. Demand, once taken away by refrigerators, has returned in a new form with the rise of subscription culture.
053.trivia: Glass bottle milk delivery has been re-evaluated in recent years due to its low environmental impact, and in the UK, the 'traditional milkman' is being re-appreciated in an eco-friendly context. It's an example of a vanished efficiency turning into an advantage as times change.

054.summary: Craftsmen of river transport who assembled felled logs into rafts or floated them individually downriver to collection points. It was a perilous logistics job, standing atop moving logs.
body: They would assemble timber felled in the mountains into rafts, or float individual logs down the river. They leaped across moving logs, using a pike pole to clear logjams stuck on rocks or in shallows. Facing rapids and cold water, with the risk of slipping and being crushed by logs—it was a job demanding both skill and courage.

timeline.text: Development of trucks and forest roads progressed.
Land transport became faster and more reliable than river transport.
Timber transport by river vanished, partly due to dam construction.

054.timelineClose: Each time a road penetrated the mountains, one less reason to transport by river disappeared. As the main mode of logistics shifted from water to land, the river-surface craftsmanship flowed away with it.
054.trivia: In Canada, there's a famous animated short and song called 'The Log Driver's Waltz,' which praises the log driver's agile movements, spinning on logs, as those of 'the best dancer.' A vanished skill lives on as a national song.

055.summary: Technicians who operated film in cinema projection booths, ensuring smooth screenings. With the transition from film to digital, their craftsmanship transformed into mere button-pressing.
body: They loaded heavy film reels onto projectors, switching between multiple machines to ensure an uninterrupted screening. They adjusted focus, brightness, and volume, paying close attention to splices where the film was prone to breaking. Unable to leave the projection booth during a screening, it was a solitary, specialized profession that supported a single film from behind the scenes.

timeline.text: The transition to Digital Cinema Package (DCP) began.
Film projectors were removed from major cinemas.
Screenings became server-based playback, eliminating the need for dedicated projectionists.

055.timelineClose: The craftsmanship of film was compressed into a single play button. It's a transformation where a specialized, qualified profession became a task combined with other duties.
055.trivia: Some directors lament the loss brought by digitalization, and a few masters still deliberately create prints for film screenings. Their dedication keeps the fading skills of projectionists alive in some theaters.

056.quote: i can write as fast as you speak
056.summary: A professional recorder who transcribed words using special symbols to keep pace with human speech. They supported the discourse of parliaments and courtrooms.
body: Using unique shorthand symbols, they transcribed statements in real-time. Attending meetings, trials, and parliamentary sessions—where accurate verbatim records were essential—they would later transcribe them into ordinary text. It was a skill, the culmination of training, to manually keep up with hundreds of words spoken per minute.

timeline.text: The spread of recording devices reduced the need for 'on-the-spot transcription'.
Voice recognition AI began to handle automatic transcription.
Specialized stenographers remain in some fields, such as court reporting.

056.timelineClose: Recording took over documentation, and AI took over transcription. Nevertheless, human judgment to accurately disentangle the complexities of spoken language is still required in some settings today.
056.trivia: In Japan's National Diet, stenographers long recorded proceedings, but in recent years, there has been a shift towards a meeting minute creation system utilizing voice recognition. The creators of democracy's primary records are quietly transitioning from humans to AI.

057.summary: A specialist who created data by punching holes in paper cards for computers to read. They were the progenitor of data entry as a profession.
body: Setting a paper card into a dedicated keypunch machine and striking a key would create a hole at that position. Computers interpreted these hole patterns as data or programs. A mistake couldn't be erased from the card—the entire card had to be re-punched.

To ensure accuracy, there was a 'verify' process where another operator would re-punch the same content for comparison. A stack (deck) of thousands of cards constituted the output of a single job, and their order was critical. It was predominantly a workplace for women.

timeline.text: Demand grew with the computerization of office work
Direct input from terminals with screens became widespread
Replaced by magnetic media and online input, cards disappeared

057.timelineClose: It was a job that bridged 'human-readable paper' and 'machine-readable holes.' When machines began accepting direct keyboard input, the bridge itself became unnecessary.
057.trivia: If a deck of cards was dropped, their order would be lost, so a diagonal line was drawn across the top edge of the deck. This allowed them to be reordered by aligning the broken line. *A programmer's worst nightmare wasn't a bug, but a staircase.*
057.lineageText: Calculator operator → Keypunch operator → Typist → Word processor operator → Data entry → LLM

058.summary: A sound artisan who created every sound effect—from doors to horse hooves to thunder—live for radio dramas. Their skills were inherited by film sound production.
body: Following the script, they'd use coconut shells for horse hooves, shake a metal sheet for thunder, and step on a gravel box for footsteps. Live broadcasts were a one-shot deal; a missed cue would ruin everything. They were magicians who conjured scenes in listeners' minds, sharing the same space as the actors' voices.

timeline.text: Radio dramas declined with the rise of television
Recorded sound effect libraries replaced live performance
The practice of live sound creation disappeared

058.timelineClose: The need to 'create sounds on the spot' vanished, but the art of making sounds by hand did not die. As Foley artists in film, they continue to record footsteps to this day.
058.trivia: The creation of live sound effects for film, known as 'Foley,' is named after Jack Foley, a pioneer in the field. Handmade sounds, almost lost in radio, survived behind the silver screen under a new name.
058.lineageText: Radio sound effects artist → Foley artist (film sound)

059.quote: the third person in the cockpit
059.summary: The third crew member in the cockpit, specializing in managing engines, fuel, and electrical systems. The electronification of instruments eliminated their seat entirely.
body: Facing the instrument panel behind the pilots, they monitored and adjusted engine output, fuel distribution, pressurization, and electrical power. They read hundreds of switches and gauges, responding immediately to any anomalies. It was a highly specialized role, solely responsible for managing the aircraft itself, allowing pilots to focus on 'flying.'
tools: Knowledge of fuel and electrical systems

timeline.text: Computer-controlled glass cockpits became practical
New aircraft designed for two-person crews (pilots only)
Computers took over the flight engineer's duties, and the seat disappeared

059.timelineClose: When systems began monitoring themselves, the human observer's seat became redundant. It's a vivid example of how computers physically eliminated a seat.
059.trivia: Pilots who had been flight engineers were highly valued for 'knowing the aircraft better than anyone.' Even as the profession disappeared, individuals with that knowledge survived by moving into the pilot's seat. The extinction was also a migration of knowledge.
059.lineageText: Flight engineer → Electronification of instruments / Two-person crew

060.summary: A clerk at a rental shop who lent out VHS tapes and DVDs. Lasting only about 30 years from its birth to its disappearance, it's a profession etched in the memory of a generation.
body: They managed shelves of new releases and recent hits, checked returned tapes for rewinding, and calculated late fees. Curating the shelves to answer customers' 'Got anything good?' was where their skill shone, and a clerk's recommendation often sparked a discovery of a new film. Friday nights were so busy the shelves would be empty.

timeline.text: Subscription streaming services began to spread
Major rental chains closed one after another
The act of 'going to rent' itself disappeared

060.timelineClose: Streaming replaced 'borrowing and returning' with 'watching anytime.' When the reason to visit a store vanished, so did the profession of the store clerk.
060.trivia: The 'Be Kind, Rewind' sticker, encouraging customers to rewind before returning, remains a nostalgic phrase symbolizing the VHS era. The very act of rewinding a tape disappeared from culture.
060.lineageText: Rental shop owner → Book rental shop owner → Video store clerk → Subscription streaming

061.summary: A technician who developed film and printed photos at DPE shops and labs in town. The entire act of 'getting film developed' disappeared with digitalization.
body: They chemically processed film in a darkroom or automatic developer, then printed it onto photographic paper. Their skill lay in correcting colors and brightness, often salvaging a difficult roll. Mini-labs at the back of camera stores boasted one-hour express development. It was also a job where they were the first to see commemorative photos from other people's lives.

timeline.text: Digital cameras rapidly became widespread
Smartphone cameras made 'shoot and share instantly' commonplace
Demand for film development plummeted, and town labs disappeared

061.timelineClose: The 'development' process itself, which existed between taking a photo and viewing it, vanished. When a process disappears, so do the professionals who performed it.
061.trivia: In recent years, film photography has seen a resurgence among young people, and development labs are quietly being re-evaluated. The skills of technicians, once almost extinct, are being rekindled modestly by the tailwind of retro hobbies.
061.lineageText: Daguerreotypist → Photo lab technician → Digital photography / Smartphones

062.quote: they said they didn't need swords anymore
062.summary: A warrior class that ruled Japan for several centuries as the dominant social stratum. They were institutionally abolished as a class during a series of Meiji reforms. It's a rare example in world history of 'the unemployment of an entire social class.'
body: In peacetime, they served as officials handling domain administration, security, and ceremonies; in wartime, they were combat personnel. Wearing a sword was a symbol of their status, and they lived on stipends (rice). They mastered literacy, martial arts, and etiquette, serving the domain as an organization—in reality, they were close to hereditary armed civil servants.

timeline.text: Domains, their employers, disappeared with the abolition of the han system
Military monopoly collapsed with conscription, and stipends were cut by the Chitsuroku Shobun
Wearing swords was prohibited by the Haitōrei, losing their symbol of status

062.timelineClose: They weren't defeated in battle, but dismissed by the system. Many samurai transitioned into civil servants, military personnel, police officers, and teachers, their education and discipline forming the backbone of the modern state.
062.trivia: Unexpected modern enterprises emerged from relief projects for unemployed samurai. Records remain across various regions of samurai descendants starting businesses or transitioning into land reclamation, tea production, and ranching. The vanished class transformed into the bearers of the next era.
062.lineageText: Samurai → Civil servants / Military personnel / Police officers

063.summary: A real-life specialized group responsible for espionage, infiltration, and sabotage. They ceded their role to modern state intelligence agencies and were reborn in the world of tourism and entertainment.
body: They infiltrated enemy territory to gather intelligence, sometimes engaging in disruption or arson. Their core skills were disguise, concealment, escape, and information transmission, rather than flashy combat. There were also long-term espionage activities where they disguised themselves as farmers or merchants and lived in enemy lands. In peacetime, it was a quiet, long-term job of delivering local intelligence to their lord.

timeline.text: Demand for wartime operations decreased in an era of peace, shifting to security and covert roles
Lost their employers with the abolition of the domains
Espionage functions transferred to modern state intelligence and police agencies

063.timelineClose: Their role didn't disappear; the bearers of that role shifted to state institutions. Simultaneously, in the popular imagination, ninja swelled into superhuman heroes, and are now global cultural icons.
063.trivia: Much of the ninja image—black attire and shuriken—was created by later plays, novels, and films. Actual shinobi primarily wore inconspicuous everyday clothes. It's a rare case where the embellished character became more famous than the true nature of the vanished profession.
063.lineageText: Ninja → Intelligence agencies (reborn in tourism and entertainment)

064.summary: An Edo-period urban transport system where two people carried a kago (palanquin) with one passenger. It was swiftly defeated by the innovation of the rickshaw.
body: They carried passengers in bamboo or wooden kago, running with two people at the front and back. Services ranged from long-distance routes connecting post towns along highways to town kago waiting for customers at street corners in castle towns. It required skill in synchronized calls and pacing, and in carrying the kago on slopes and rough roads. Speed and comfort determined a kago bearer's reputation.

timeline.text: The rickshaw was invented
Rickshaws, which could transport people more easily and quickly with wheels, rapidly replaced kago
Kago bearers transitioned to rickshaw pullers

064.timelineClose: It was faster, easier, and cheaper for 'a person to pull a cart' than for 'people to carry a person.' Even with the same human power, the simple innovation of the wheel eliminated the traditional profession.
064.trivia: There's an anecdote that the Japanese inventor of the rickshaw conceived it after observing the inefficiency of kago bearers. *The bearers of the old profession survived by switching to the next mode of transport—the lineage of transportation continued from carriers to pullers.*

065.summary: Edo's communication infrastructure, delivering letters and money on foot. It's the origin point of a lineage where the 'demand for transport' is immortal, only its form continuously changes.
body: They carried letters, money orders, and small packages, running from post town to post town, or covering long distances in relays. Strong legs, capable of running through the night, crossing rivers, and traversing mountains, were their capital. There were various types: *tsugi-hikyaku* for public use, those exclusively for daimyo, and *machi-hikyaku* for commoners. Some express services connected Edo and Osaka in just a few days. It was also a business built on trust.
tools: knowledge of highways and post towns

timeline.text: Modern postal system is established
Government-run postal service with nationwide uniform rates replaces hikyaku couriers
Some hikyaku agencies transform into transportation and freight companies

065.timelineClose: From running humans to systems and railways. Yet, the demand to 'deliver quickly and reliably' never died, continuing to evolve into postal services, parcel delivery, and food delivery, running all the way to today.
065.trivia: Among the hikyaku agencies, some rode the wave of modernization to develop into major logistics companies that continue to this day. The genes of the strong legs that ran through Edo now live on in trucks and delivery apps.
065.lineageText: Hikyaku courier → Postal service → Parcel delivery → Food delivery

066.summary: Edo's news vendor, who sold printed sheets detailing incidents and disasters while reading them aloud on the streets. They are the ancestor of Japanese journalism.
body: Fires, double suicides, vendettas, earthquakes—they hastily printed events that stirred public interest using clay or woodblocks, then stood on the streets in pairs. One would read aloud in an engaging manner, while the other sold, creating crowds in this 'yomiuri' (reading and selling) style. It was a media of instant impact, where timeliness and sensationalism dictated sales.

timeline.text: Newspapers using letterpress printing are launched
Periodical newspapers surpass kawaraban in timeliness and comprehensiveness
Street-side reading and selling is absorbed by newspapers

066.timelineClose: Irregular single-sheet prints couldn't compete with daily newspapers. However, the knack for 'attracting people with shocking headlines' was firmly inherited by subsequent media.
