066.trivia: Kawaraban were often unofficial and illegal publications by the shogunate, sold with authors and publishers concealed to evade crackdowns. Japanese scoop reporting, from its very beginning, existed in a tense relationship with the authorities.

067.quote: i'll tie a stylish topknot for you
067.summary: A specialist profession in Edo that styled and maintained people's topknots. Triggered by legal decrees, it transformed, and its skills persisted as the barber and beauty industry.
body: The *mawari-kamiyui*, who shaved men's foreheads (sakayaki) and styled their topknots, traveled to clients' homes or barbershops with their toolboxes. Female *onna-kamiyui* were highly skilled professionals who created intricate shimada and marumage styles. In a society where hairstyles indicated status, age, and marital status, the kamiyui's job was to manage the symbolic language of appearance.

timeline.text: Sanpatsu Datto Rei (Decree to Cut Hair and Remove Swords) is issued, allowing topknots to be cut
Westernization (Bunmei Kaika) popularizes short hair and Western hairstyles, reducing demand for topknots
Kamiyui transform their business into barbers and beauticians

067.timelineClose: 'Tap a short-cropped head, and you'll hear the sound of civilization's dawn'—the sound sung in that song was also the sound of the kamiyui's profession transforming. Their techniques were passed down to modern barbering and beauty.
067.trivia: Female kamiyui were, for a time, subject to prohibitions as their services were deemed a luxury. There was an era when common women spending money on their hair was regulated as a matter of public morals.

068.summary: The pride of Edo, the town firefighters (*machi-hikeshi*) who specialized in destructive firefighting. Their organization transitioned into modern fire departments, and their spirit was inherited by firefighters.
body: Their main strategy during fires was 'destructive firefighting,' using *tobiguchi* (fire hooks) to demolish houses downwind before the flames spread, thereby preventing further conflagration. They contained fires in densely packed wooden areas, where water was ineffective, by cutting off the path of the flames. Each group competed to be first, raising their *matoi* (standard), and the *matoi-mochi* (standard-bearer) who waved it on rooftops was a star. Many of them were originally construction workers (tobi).

timeline.text: Fire brigades are institutionalized and reorganized into modern organizations
Water discharge firefighting using pumps replaces destructive firefighting
Incorporated into the system as permanent fire departments and firefighters

068.timelineClose: The target to extinguish remained the same, but the method changed from 'destroying' to 'spraying water.' The profession didn't vanish; it's a transformed type where the organization and technology modernized.
068.trivia: The *matoi*, a symbol of the hikeshi, is still waved today by fire brigades and at New Year's fire review ceremonies. The spirit of Edo's hikeshi lives on in modern fire culture as ritual and traditional art.

069.summary: An unofficial investigator privately employed by a *dōshin* (low-ranking samurai police officer), serving as their eyes and hands for urban investigations and arrests. Modern police absorbed this role.
body: They held an unofficial status, privately hired by *dōshin* from the magistrate's office, with their wages paid out of the *dōshin*'s own pocket. Well-versed in local affairs, they handled interrogations, stakeouts, and the apprehension of criminals. Many were former members of the underworld whose information networks were valued, and being entrusted with a *jitte* (truncheon) was a mark of their authority.

timeline.text: Modern police system begins to be established
Official positions like *rasotsu* (police officers) and *junsa* (patrolmen) take over investigations
The position of unofficial operative is eliminated from the system

069.timelineClose: The ambiguous status of 'privately hired investigative operative' was replaced by a public police organization. The work of investigation remained; only the unofficial nature of the status disappeared.
069.trivia: While *okappiki* are portrayed as heroes of justice in period dramas, in reality, they often engaged in extortion-like behavior and were frequently subject to prohibitions. The modern state reorganized these individuals, who were half-outlaws, into its institutional framework.

070.summary: A hereditary specialist profession in Nagasaki during Japan's isolationist period, handling Dutch and Chinese interpretation and trade affairs. The *sakoku* (isolation) system created it, and the opening of the country dismantled it.
body: They were responsible for negotiations with the Dutch trading post in Dejima, translating trade documents, and collecting and reporting overseas information. Language skills were passed down from parent to child as a family profession, acquired through oral tradition and practical experience in an era without dictionaries. Beyond mere interpretation, they served as a narrow window for isolated Japan, conveying Western scholarship and world affairs to the shogunate.

timeline.text: The opening of the country breaks Nagasaki's monopoly on trade
Interpreters who studied English and other languages in Western-style schools emerge across the country
From a hereditary privileged profession to an open interpretation and translation industry

070.timelineClose: The *sakoku* system, with its 'only one window,' created the privilege of the *tsūji*. When all windows opened, the guardian of a specific window became unnecessary. However, the linguistic skills were inherited by modern interpreters.
070.trivia: The *tsūji* were unsung heroes of Japan's modernization, greatly contributing to the adoption of Dutch Studies (*Rangaku*) and Western medicine. Some of the words they translated remain as academic terms in Japanese today.

071.summary: Edo's rental business, which lent everything from futons to clothing and tools. They are the ancestor of 'consumption without ownership.'
body: They rented out a full range of daily necessities for a fee. Items varied widely, from futons, pots and pans, and clothing, to formal wear for celebrations and funerals, and even carpentry tools. For Edo commoners living in small *nagaya* (row houses) who owned few possessions, borrowing only when needed was rational. 'Sonryō' referred to the fee for wear and tear from use.

timeline.text: Industrialization makes daily necessities affordable
'Ownership' becomes a symbol of wealth
Sonryōya disappear, but their lineage continues in rental bookshops and others

071.timelineClose: Mass production created an era where 'buying was cheaper than borrowing,' diminishing the need for rentals. Yet, the philosophy of 'not owning' never died, connecting to rental bookshops, general rentals, and modern subscriptions.
071.trivia: Edo was one of the world's leading recycling and rental cities. Sonryōya, used clothing stores, and repair shops flourished, establishing a circular economy where goods were used to their fullest. 'Living without owning' was not a new philosophy, but an everyday reality in Edo.
071.lineageText: Sonryōya → Rental bookshop → Video rental → Subscription service

072.summary: The basic form of a small-scale merchant who carried goods suspended from a carrying pole (tenbinbō) and walked through town, selling with a distinctive call. They are the archetype of all itinerant vendors.
body: Fish, vegetables, tofu, shijimi clams, natto—they procured only what could be carried on a single *tenbinbō* and went through the alleys of *nagaya* (row houses) with their unique selling calls. Since it required little capital to start, it became an occupation for people migrating into the city. It was a familiar business, visiting regular customers, where their voice and route were their assets.

timeline.text: Permanent retail stores increase
Supermarkets appear, and shopping shifts to stores
From mobile vending to fixed stores, and then to online retail

072.timelineClose: The business of 'sellers going to customers' was replaced by 'customers coming to stores.' However, in recent years, the business of 'delivering to customers' is seeing a resurgence in the form of mobile vending and online retail.
072.trivia: The *botefuri*'s unique selling calls had specific melodies for each product, so one could tell what was being sold just by the voice, even without seeing them. The soundscape of the city itself was a living advertisement.
072.lineageText: Botefuri peddler → Itinerant vendor → Retail store → Supermarket → Online retail

073.summary: A seasonal peddler who walked the summer streets, carrying goldfish in tubs on a shoulder pole, calling out 'goldfish, oh, goldfish~'. Their cry was a soundscape of summer.
body: On summer afternoons, they would carry shallow tubs of swimming goldfish on their shoulders, selling them to people seeking a moment of cool. Goldfish became a popular pastime during the Edo period, their graceful swimming a quintessential summer sight. Their drawn-out, leisurely calls would melt into the hot afternoon air.

timeline.text: Pet shops and festivals became sources for goldfish
Changes in lifestyle reduced the number of itinerant peddlers
The goldfish peddler's cry vanished from the streets

073.timelineClose: The trade that carried the seasons with its calls lost its place due to the diversification of shops and entertainment. Its memory barely lingers on at goldfish scooping stalls.
073.trivia: The goldfish peddler's cry was immortalized in rakugo and haiku, treated almost like a kigo (seasonal word) for summer. It was a peddling trade where the sound became part of the culture even before the sight—the sound itself is a monument to this vanished occupation.
073.lineageText: Goldfish peddler → Pet shops, festival stalls

074.quote: feeling tired? let me massage you.
074.summary: A practitioner who relieved body stiffness through massage therapy. Many were visually impaired, and this profession served as a form of occupational security for them. It was later incorporated into the system as a national qualification.
body: They would wander the night streets, blowing a whistle, then enter a client's home to provide a full-body massage. The treatment, which relieved stiffness and fatigue through acupressure and manual techniques, relied entirely on experience and the sense of touch. During the Edo period, it was protected as a vital livelihood for the visually impaired, and they even had their own professional organizations.

timeline.text: A qualification system for practitioners was established
Anma Massage Shiatsu Therapist was designated as a national qualification
The 'itinerant anma' transformed into qualified practitioners

074.timelineClose: Rather than the profession vanishing, it was elevated within the system. While the form of wandering the night streets disappeared, the manual techniques themselves were established as a nationally qualified specialized profession.
074.trivia: The sound of the anma masseur's whistle was a familiar feature of the night streets. This tone, known as the 'anma whistle,' was an auditory signboard, announcing the arrival of the unseen practitioner to clients.
074.lineageText: Anma masseur → Anma Massage Shiatsu Therapist (national qualification)

075.summary: An Edo-period human resources brokerage that mediated between servants and employers. It was the prototype of the modern HR business.
body: They would mediate and introduce servants, maids, and laborers needed by samurai families and merchants to job seekers. They also provided background checks and earned a referral fee. It was an information brokerage that understood both the inner workings of the workplaces and the character of the job seekers, making trust the lifeline of their business. Some also handled the arrangement of day laborers.
tools: Job vacancy and job seeker information

timeline.text: Modern job placement systems began to take shape
Public employment agencies and private HR companies were institutionalized
Brokerage services evolved into public employment offices and HR agencies

075.timelineClose: The demand for 'connecting people with jobs' is immortal, but the providers shifted from individual businesses to institutions and corporations. The problems of intermediary exploitation, which became a concern, spurred this institutionalization.
075.trivia: Kuchiireya were also called 'Keian.' One theory suggests this name originated from a person who arranged marriages and service. The job of talent placement has continued for centuries, changing its name along the way.
075.lineageText: Kuchiireya → Public employment offices, HR agencies

076.summary: A male professional entertainer who mediated between guests and geisha at banquets, enlivening the atmosphere. The term 'taikomochi' now only remains as an idiom, with only a few active practitioners left nationwide.
body: They were called to banquets at ryotei restaurants and tatami rooms, where they would liven up the party with storytelling, dance, and hidden talents. It was a sophisticated form of hospitality entertainment, involving elevating the guests, highlighting the geisha, and creating laughter by reading the room. The knack for enlivening the mood without offending guests was a professional art that couldn't be mastered overnight.

timeline.text: The hanamachi (geisha district) and ryotei culture itself declined
Styles of entertaining and banquets changed, and demand dwindled
Only a few active practitioners remain nationwide

076.timelineClose: As the 'workplace' of banquets shrank, the arts that could only thrive there also lost their place. 'Taikomochi' only remains in everyday language as a metaphor for someone who flatters.
076.trivia: Contrary to the image conjured by the term 'taikomochi,' the art of the hōkan was a sophisticated form of storytelling, rich in culture and wit. The fact that it became synonymous with flattery might be the greatest misunderstanding of this profession.
076.lineageText: Taikomochi → (A few continue as hospitality entertainers)

077.quote: take a peek, a story awaits.
077.summary: A street spectacle that showed a continuous picture story through a lens in a peep-hole box. It was the great-grandfather of video media.
body: They would show enlarged pictures, set inside a large box, through a lens in a peep-hole. The operator would narrate the story with a distinctive rhythm, pulling strings to change the pictures one after another. With narratives and music accompanying sequential illustrations depicting tragic love or incidents, a complete drama unfolded within the small hole.

timeline.text: Moving pictures (cinema) appeared
Moving images on screens overwhelmed sequential still images
Street peep shows disappeared

077.timelineClose: The spectacle of one person at a time peeking into a hole couldn't compete with movies, which many people could watch simultaneously. The desire to 'show stories with pictures' expanded its vessel from peep-holes to screens.
077.trivia: The unique narrative rhythm of the nozoki karakuri is partially preserved in records as 'nozoki-bushi.' The style of narration accompanying visuals was later inherited by katsudō benshi (silent film narrators). Within the peep-hole lay the prototype of the movie theater.
077.lineageText: Peep show operator → Katsudō benshi → Cinema → Television

078.quote: the rest of the story, in kōshaku.
078.summary: A storyteller who narrated war tales and kōdan (storytelling) on the streets, earning tips. It evolved into an indoor performing art called 'kōdan' and continues to exist as a traditional performing art.
body: Standing on streets or in squares, they would narrate war tales like 'Taiheiki' or heroic sagas, tapping a lectern. With intonation, pauses, and the sound of their harisen (paper fan), they would draw the audience into the story, cutting off at a crucial moment to encourage tips. It was a street live performance that gathered people for free and opened their wallets with storytelling artistry.

timeline.text: Permanent entertainment venues called yose (storytelling halls) were established
Radio and television became the center of entertainment
It moved from the streets to indoor 'kōdan,' continuing as a traditional performing art

078.timelineClose: The open-air, tip-based profession gave way to yose (storytelling halls) that charged admission and to broadcast entertainment. However, the art of storytelling itself did not die, but has been passed down to this day as kōdanshi (kōdan storytellers).
078.trivia: In recent years, kōdan has regained attention with the emergence of young performers, attracting new audiences at yose and through streaming. One could say that the art of storytelling, which began on the streets, has come full circle, returning to a 'new street' in the form of streaming.

079.summary: A peddler who walked around selling household remedies with the cry 'any antidotes needed?' Many were women from farming villages, working as migrant laborers during the off-season.
body: Women would pack antidotes (folk remedies believed to be effective for food poisoning, etc.) made in production areas like Echigo into wicker trunks, carrying them to sell far and wide. It was a valuable source of cash income during the agricultural off-season, and their distinctive calls and kasuri (ikat) attire were a familiar sight of itinerant trade. It was a business built on trust and familiarity, visiting regular customers every year.

timeline.text: The pharmaceutical system was developed, and drug distribution modernized
Pharmacy and pharmaceutical company products became widespread in households
Itinerant medicine peddlers disappeared

079.timelineClose: The household medicine cabinet shifted from itinerant peddlers to products from pharmacies and pharmaceutical manufacturers. Institutionalized pharmaceutical distribution absorbed the simple folk medicine peddling.
079.trivia: The Echigo antidote peddlers were even sung about in folk songs, supporting the regional economy as a collective migrant labor force of women. More than the medicine itself, the memory of the women who carried it remains more vivid.

080.quote: you only pay for what you use.
080.summary: 'Use first, pay later'—an itinerant medicine peddler who left medicines in homes and collected payment only for what was used later. It was a system that could be called the Edo-period version of a subscription service, and it continues to a small extent even today.
body: They would leave medicine chests in each household, visiting once or twice a year to settle accounts for used medicines and replenish supplies. It was a 'pay-later for what you use' model based on trust, and they traveled to customers nationwide. They also brought small gifts like paper balloons for children and carried local news, with community ties forming the foundation of their business.

timeline.text: Drugstores and online retail made medicines easily accessible
The market is shrinking along with its aging customer base
Ongoing as a household medicine business, albeit on a reduced scale

080.timelineClose: This advanced model of 'use when needed, pay only for what's used' is ironically being pushed aside by the convenience of retail stores and online shopping. The system itself isn't outdated, but it's a transformation and contraction where the practitioners are dwindling.
080.trivia: 'Use first, pay later' is a system that delivers products based on customer trust, an idea akin to modern subscriptions and freemium models. The prototype of today's business models existed in Toyama 300 years ago.
080.lineageText: Toyama medicine peddler → Household medicine business (contracting, ongoing)

081.summary: The rickshaw puller transported passengers by pulling the rickshaw, an invention of Meiji-era Japan. Today, the profession has been reborn as a sightseeing attraction in places like Asakusa and Kamakura.
body: Carrying passengers in a two-wheeled rickshaw, they ran on foot, pulling the vehicle themselves. Faster and cheaper than palanquins, rickshaws became the main mode of urban transport during the Meiji era. Strong legs and endurance were their capital, along with an intimate knowledge of the city's geography and shortcuts. They earned more on rainy days or with urgent customers. Some belonged to rickshaw stations, while others roamed the streets to pick up fares.

timeline.text: Streetcars, buses, and taxis become widespread
Automobile transport replaces rickshaws
Reborn as an experiential service in tourist areas

081.timelineClose: Though defeated by automobiles as a means of transport, the very act of being 'pulled by a person' regained value as an emotional experience. It was a splendid transformation from a practical vehicle to a tourist attraction.
081.trivia: Rickshaws were exported from Japan to China and Southeast Asia, becoming a staple of urban transport in various regions. The English word "rickshaw" originates from the Japanese "jinrikisha" (人力車). A Japanese invention, along with its name, became a global word.
081.lineageText: Palanquin bearer → Rickshaw puller → Taxi driver (survives as sightseeing rickshaw)

082.summary: The packhorse driver was a key figure in land transport, leading horses laden with goods. Their image lives on in the proverb, "Even a packhorse driver looks good in fine clothes."
body: They loaded goods onto a horse's back and led it along highways and mountain paths to its destination. This ranged from long-distance material transport to relaying goods between post towns. It required skill in managing the horse's health, loading cargo, and handling difficult roads. The 'mago-uta' (packhorse driver's songs), sung to soothe the horses while walking, remain as folk songs in various regions.

timeline.text: Trucks and railway freight become widespread
Automobile transport replaces horse-drawn carriage
Packhorse drivers transform into the trucking industry

082.timelineClose: Engines replaced horses. The work of transporting remained, but the power source shifted from living creatures to machines. It marks a single waypoint in the lineage of logistics.
082.trivia: The proverb "Mago ni mo isho" (馬子にも衣装) means that even a person of low status, like a packhorse driver, can look respectable when dressed up. The proverb preserves the social standing of a past occupation.

083.quote: to the other side, in a flash!
083.summary: The ferryman transported people and goods across rivers where there were no bridges. With each bridge built, one by one, they disappeared.
body: At river crossings, they operated oars and poles to carry passengers and cargo to the opposite bank. Their skill lay in reading changes in water levels and currents to ensure a safe crossing. Key points where highways were cut off by rivers always had a ferry crossing, and ferrymen served as crucial nodes in local transport. It was a job of constantly traversing the same river from morning till night.

timeline.text: Bridge construction progresses across the country
Ferry crossings are replaced by bridges with road network development
Ferry services disappear

083.timelineClose: Permanent infrastructure like bridges rendered the human service of the ferryman unnecessary. The completion of a single bridge quietly ended a single ferry crossing and the ferryman's profession.
083.trivia: Even today, a very small number of ferry services remain as tourist attractions or essential local transport. Terrain unsuitable for bridges, or a deliberate desire to preserve a nostalgic crossing, keep the last vestiges of this vanished profession alive.

084.quote: bring on the cargo, right on my shoulder!
084.summary: Stevedores were port workers who manually loaded and unloaded ship cargo. The advent of the container, a 'standardized unit,' completely eliminated this heavy labor.
body: Between the docked ship and the quay, they carried and stacked various types of cargo—sacks, wooden boxes, hemp bags—using sheer manpower. It required physical strength to carry heavy loads and the wisdom to efficiently stack diverse bulk cargo in the ship's hold. Each port had its own labor gangs, and systems for hiring day laborers were well-developed.

timeline.text: Containerization of maritime transport spreads globally
Gantry cranes handle standardized boxes mechanically
Manual loading and unloading drastically decreases

084.timelineClose: By standardizing cargo into 'uniform boxes,' the need for human carrying disappeared. This is a rare example where an idea—a 'standard'—rather than a technology, eliminated a massive amount of labor.
084.trivia: The container revolution drastically reduced port workers while dramatically lowering shipping costs and accelerating globalization. The invention of a single standard reshaped both the landscape of labor and the global economy.
084.lineageText: Stevedore → Gantry cranes and port mechanization

085.summary: Station porters, identifiable by their red caps, carried passengers' luggage at train stations. They were, in a sense, the Japanese equivalent of Pullman porters.
body: On station platforms and within the station premises, they carried passengers' heavy luggage and trunks to their designated trains or taxis. Wearing red caps, they waited for customers, with tips being their primary income. In an era when luggage was heavy and bulky, and travel was a major undertaking, station porters were reliable helpers for travelers.

timeline.text: Suitcases with casters become widespread
Coin lockers and parcel delivery services solve luggage problems
Station porters disappear from stations

085.timelineClose: The demand for 'having heavy luggage carried' was eliminated by wheeled bags and parcel delivery services. Travel luggage became lighter, and there was no longer a need to rely on others.
085.trivia: The name of the light freight transport company "Akabou" (赤帽, Red Cap) originates from these station porters. The red cap, once a symbol of luggage carrying, now continues to run as a brand name for a different transport service.
085.lineageText: Station porter → Coin lockers and parcel delivery services

086.summary: Bus conductors were onboard staff responsible for collecting fares and providing in-bus announcements. The "bus girl" was also an admired profession. They disappeared with the shift to one-man operated buses.
body: Inside a moving bus, they collected fares, punched tickets, announced stops, and safely guided passengers on and off. Giving the departure signal was also the conductor's role. Their agile movements in uniform symbolized the new working women of the city. They operated each bus as a team of two with the driver.

timeline.text: One-man operated buses are introduced
Fare boxes, numbered tickets, and automatic announcements replace conductors
Conductors disappear from buses

086.timelineClose: Machines took over fare collection and announcements, turning a two-person team into one. IC cards and automatic announcements continue to carry on the work of the vanished conductor today.
086.trivia: In the early Showa era, "bus girls" were a popular and glamorous profession, known for their modern uniforms. They were even sung about in popular songs of the time, symbolizing a new image of working women. This admired profession disappeared as a typical example of mechanization.
086.lineageText: Bus conductor → One-man operated buses → IC cards

087.summary: Tram drivers operated streetcars that ran through the heart of the city. The extensive network of Tokyo's trams was progressively abolished with the increase in automobiles.
body: Gripping the master controller and brake handle, they operated electric trains running in the middle of the road. As cars, bicycles, and pedestrians shared the same road surface, they constantly had to pay attention to their surroundings while maintaining scheduled operations. Speed on curves, braking in the rain, managing passenger boarding and alighting during congestion—this was the skill required to make urban transport function as a 'railway on the road'.
They operated each tram as a team of two with a conductor, and the 'chin-chin' bell signal for departure became part of the city's soundscape.

timeline.text: Automobiles rapidly increase, and streetcars are deemed a cause of traffic jams
Most Tokyo tram lines are abolished*
Urban transport shifts to subways and buses

087.timelineClose: It wasn't that the trams became an obstacle, but that the main player on the roads changed. In recent years, streetcars (LRT) are being re-evaluated for environmental reasons, and the decision to abolish them is itself being questioned.
087.trivia: In Tokyo, only the Arakawa Line (Tokyo Sakura Tram) survives, with drivers still actively operating it today. A line on the verge of complete abolition has, conversely, become a cherished and valuable tourist resource.
087.lineageText: Tram driver → Subways and buses (survives on some lines)

088.quote: shovel the coal, time to depart!
088.summary: Steam locomotives were operated by a two-person crew: a fireman who shoveled coal and an engineer who controlled the engine. Today, the preservation of these skills has become a tourist attraction.
body: The fireman continuously shoveled coal into the furnace with a scoop, maintaining a constant steam pressure. Poor shoveling would reduce power, causing the train to stall on inclines. The engineer, monitoring pressure and speed, operated the regulator valve to keep the train on schedule. The cab was a fiery hell even in summer, and tunnels filled with smoke.
Coal, water, fire—it was a job of conversing with a machine that felt alive.

timeline.text: Electrification and dieselization progress under the modernization plan
Regular steam locomotive operations on JNR main lines end*
Skills are preserved for the operation of sightseeing SLs

088.timelineClose: A machine that lost on efficiency was revived by sentiment. A reversal phenomenon is occurring, where the skills of firemen are deliberately passed down for SL operations.
088.trivia: For the revival of SL operations, scenes of retired engineers teaching young drivers can be seen across the country. A vanished profession has been called back as a teacher of a vanished profession.
088.lineageText: Steam locomotive crew → Electric train driver (skills preserved for sightseeing SLs)

089.summary: A guardian who manually raised and lowered the crossing gates every time a train approached. Once, people stood at railway crossings across the country.
body: Stationed in a small hut beside the crossing, they learned of approaching trains from electric bells or timetables, then turned a handle to lower the gates. After confirming passage, they raised them again. This cycle continued all day long—through rain, snow, and late into the night. It was a monotonous job that demanded constant vigilance, as a momentary lapse in judgment could directly lead to loss of life.

timeline.text: Installation of automatic crossing alarms and gates progresses
Keepers gradually disappear from railway crossings nationwide
Number of crossings themselves decreasing due to grade separation

089.timelineClose: Machines don't tire or doze off. Monotonous surveillance tasks related to safety became the top priority for automation.
089.trivia: The crossing keeper's hut often featured a garden tended by the keeper or a pet cat. A job spent all day in the same spot often led to transforming that place into one's own garden.
089.lineageText: Crossing keeper → Automatic crossing gate → Grade separation

090.summary: Before automatic ticket gates, station staff stood at the turnstiles, punching each passenger's ticket. The click-clack echoing through the rush-hour gates was the very sound of the station.
body: Standing at the ticket gate, they received tickets, punched a hole with their ticket punch, and returned them. During rush hour, this meant more than one ticket per second. To maintain the flow, they would click-clack the punch even when no tickets were presented, keeping their rhythm. That sound wasn't a habit, but a technique to keep their hands moving.

At the same time, their job involved instantly checking the ticket's route and date, and spotting 'kiseru' (fare evasion). They were artisans of dynamic vision and memory, capable of instantly distinguishing hundreds of different ticket types.

timeline.text: World's first automatic ticket gate installed at Hankyu Kita-Senri Station
Automatic ticket gates simultaneously introduced to JR and private railways in the Tokyo metropolitan area
With the advent of IC cards, physical tickets themselves begin to decline

090.timelineClose: The sound of the ticket punch almost entirely vanished from across the country at the beginning of the Heisei era. Today, the legacy of 'punching' faintly lives on in the stamps received at manned gates.
090.trivia: The shape of the hole punched by the ticket punch actually differed from station to station. Round, triangular, house-shaped—this was to identify which station a ticket passed through and prevent fraud. 'Punch mark collections,' featuring these unique cut-out shapes, still exist in the world of railway enthusiasts today.
090.lineageText: Ticket puncher → Automatic ticket gate → IC card → Facial recognition gate

091.summary: An attendant who pushed passengers into crowded train doors. Still found at some stations, they represent a 'peculiar Japanese job' from an overseas perspective.
body: Standing on the platform during rush hour, they pushed passengers into the train when the doors wouldn't close. Though it might look rough, they were actually safety personnel, preventing passengers from getting caught, ensuring door safety, and prompting departure. Their job wasn't just to push, but also to judge when 'no more is possible' and direct passengers to the next train.
Many were student part-timers or station staff performing dual roles.

timeline.text: Became established with the intensification of commuter rush hour
Need decreases with the installation of platform doors and increased transport capacity
Rush hour itself is changing with the establishment of remote work

091.timelineClose: If the premise of crowded trains collapses, the job of pushing will also disappear. When 'ways of working' change, the 'jobs that support those ways of working' also vanish—a domino effect.
091.trivia: Overseas media have symbolically reported on Japan's commuter scene as 'oshiya.' What was an everyday sight for Japanese people was a peculiar spectacle from the outside—the meaning of a profession changes with perspective.
091.lineageText: Train pusher → Platform doors / Increased transport capacity / Remote work

092.summary: Mountain folk who felled giant trees with only an axe and a saw. Chainsaws and high-performance forestry machinery rendered their skills a thing of the past.
body: Entering the mountains, they would read the tree's lean, the wind, and the terrain to determine the felling direction, then create a notch with an axe and make a back cut with a saw. Felling a single tree took several hours, and a misjudgment could cost a life. They often lived in groups, staying overnight in the mountains, and were a professional collective with their own unique customs and language.

timeline.text: Chainsaws become widespread, felling speed skyrockets
High-performance forestry machinery mechanizes everything from felling to hauling
Hand tool skills remain in some specialized fields and cultural heritage restoration

092.timelineClose: The evolution of tools rendered skills learned by hand unnecessary. However, the eye for reading trees cannot be replaced by machines, and that aspect alone is still passed down among foresters today.
092.trivia: Soma treated the mountains as sacred and performed rituals to the mountain gods before felling trees. This custom of accompanying the act of felling with reverence was wisdom born from a life-threatening profession.

093.summary: A profession that dug coal hundreds of meters underground, supporting Japan's modern industry. The history of mine closures is also the history of the disappearance of entire communities.
body: They descended hundreds of meters into the mine shafts by trolley and on foot, wielding pickaxes and rock drills in dark, narrow, hot coal faces. Cave-ins, flooding, gas explosions—they were constantly living alongside death, and accidents claimed dozens of lives at once. Coal towns were complete with company housing, shops, and even cinemas, forming a living sphere where a single company encompassed an entire town.

timeline.text: Energy revolution shifts primary energy source from coal to oil
Coal mines across the country close one after another
Last major underground coal mine in Japan closes*

093.timelineClose: When a profession disappears, it's not always just the profession itself that vanishes. The closure of coal mines erased entire towns, schools, and shopping streets from the map. A shift in energy policy folded up entire communities.
093.trivia: The sites of former coal towns are now sometimes registered as World Heritage industrial sites. The ruins of towns abandoned by people are revisited as tourist resources—the record of disappearance has become a new value.
093.lineageText: Coal miner → Oil and electricity industries

094.quote: i'll dig until water comes out
094.summary: An artisan who manually dug dozens of meters vertically into the ground to find water veins. One by one, they went out of business as piped water arrived.
body: They read the water veins from the land's topography and geology, then dug a narrow hole vertically downwards. It was a collaborative effort between the digger below and the one pulling up soil above. The deeper they went, the thinner the oxygen and the greater the risk of collapse. It was also a job with an element of gamble, as they weren't paid until water emerged. The intuition to strike a water vein determined an artisan's reputation.

timeline.text: Laying of water supply systems progresses from urban areas
Piped water spreads to rural areas, demand for wells disappears
Mechanical boring replaces specialized manual work

094.timelineClose: Turn a tap and water comes out—as this commonplace became widespread, the job of digging for water disappeared. Like water sellers, it was a profession absorbed by infrastructure.
094.trivia: Well diggers marketed their ability to 'strike water veins,' and some even used divinatory methods. Before science, groundwater exploration relied on experience, intuition, and a touch of mysticism.
094.lineageText: Water seller → Well digger → Piped water infrastructure

095.summary: A lodging business that provided rooms and meals to students and single individuals. It was a form of housing from an era when landlords acted as surrogate parents.
body: They rented out part of their home, cooked breakfast and dinner, drew baths, and handled visitors and phone calls. They set curfews, monitored behavior, and sometimes wrote letters to the boarders' parents. It was less about renting a room and more about taking on an entire lifestyle. Interactions between boarders also fostered a kind of surrogate family.

timeline.text: One-room apartments with baths and toilets become widespread
Values emphasizing privacy become prevalent
Boarding houses with meals almost entirely disappear

095.timelineClose: The 'hassle of living with others' could now be avoided with money. However, the demand for connected living, in the form of share houses, is returning in a different guise.
095.trivia: The boarding houses where literary giants and artists spent their youth are now popular spots for literary walks. A room in a humble lodging becomes a monument as the birthplace of later Japanese literature—places outlive professions.
095.lineageText: Boarding house keeper → Rental apartment → Share house

096.summary: During an era when newspaper companies used pigeons to transport manuscripts and photographic film, this was a dedicated attendant who raised and flew pigeons in a rooftop dovecote.
body: They maintained a dovecote on the company building's rooftop, training and managing hundreds of pigeons. When a reporter released a pigeon from the field with a communication tube containing manuscripts or film attached to its leg, the pigeon would fly straight back to headquarters. It was a specialized avian profession, responsible for pigeon health management, training flights, and even bloodline management.
They supported breaking news from places without telephone lines, such as mountains or disaster sites.

timeline.text: Telephone lines and wireless communication become widespread nationwide
Phototelegraphy technology becomes practical
Newspaper company dovecotes are closed down

096.timelineClose: Wires were faster and more reliable than living creatures. Yet, anecdotes persist in various companies that when communication networks failed during disasters, it was the pigeons that flew until the very end.
096.trivia: Records remain of pigeons playing active roles in breaking news from the Olympics, mountain climbing expeditions, and crime scenes. The newspaper companies' race for breaking news was once also a race of pigeon speed and homing instinct.
096.lineageText: Express messenger → Carrier pigeon handler → Telephone / Wireless → Internet connection

097.summary: A specialist who meticulously transcribed documents using a typewriter. From a glamorous skilled profession to a fundamental skill for all humanity—even removed from census classifications.
body: Typists accurately transcribed handwritten manuscripts onto typewriters. Japanese typists performed a skilled craft, selecting each character from a vast type plate, while English typists competed on speed and accuracy. Mistakes were irreversible, often requiring an entire page to be retyped. All corporate documents passed through the hands of typists, and dedicated typing rooms were common.

timeline.text: Word processors become widespread
Personal computers become ubiquitous, ushering in an era where everyone types for themselves
'Word Processor Operator' is removed from census occupational classifications

097.timelineClose: Typing transitioned from a specialized profession to a universal skill. Like the scribe, it didn't vanish, but rather was distributed among all humanity.
097.trivia: Japanese typewriters required selecting each character from a type plate with over 2,000 characters, meaning even skilled operators could only type a few dozen characters per minute. Yet, it was considered 'more beautiful and formal' than handwriting, and public documents were typed.
097.lineageText: Calculator Operator → Keypuncher → Typist → Word Processor Operator → Voice Recognition AI

098.summary: A craftsperson who unstitched kimonos, returned them to a single piece of fabric, washed and stretched them on boards to dry, then re-sewed them. Their fate was intertwined with kimono culture.
body: They would unpick a kimono, returning it to its original bolt of fabric, wash it with water, apply starch, and stretch it on bamboo rods (shinshi) or boards to dry. The skill lay in preserving the fabric's texture and restoring its dimensions. Once dry, it would be re-sewn into a kimono. This was an indispensable maintenance service for traditional Japanese attire, allowing kimonos to be worn for a lifetime.

timeline.text: Western clothing becomes widespread as daily wear
Synthetic fibers and dry cleaners transform garment care
A few survive as specialist kimono care shops (shikkaiya)

098.timelineClose: When what we wear changes, so too does the work of caring for it. The foundation of this profession disappeared the moment the custom of unpicking and washing kimonos annually ceased to be a part of daily life.
098.trivia: Arai-hari was central to the system of using a single piece of kimono fabric for decades by 'unpicking, washing, and re-sewing' it. This ultimate sustainable clothing culture, continuing since the Edo period, was supported by the existence of this specialized profession.
098.lineageText: Kimono Washer → Dry Cleaner (a few survive as shikkaiya)

099.summary: The village's all-purpose metalworker, who forged and repaired everything from farm tools to knives and metal fittings. Pressured by factory production, the craft continues faintly as a traditional art.
body: Heating iron red in the forge, hammering it on the anvil, quenching it in water—this cycle created hoes, sickles, and knives. They also undertook repairs of broken farm tools, meeting all the village's metal needs. The 'ton-ten-kan' sound of the hammer echoed through the settlement, and the blacksmith's forge was also a gathering place for people.

timeline.text: Factory-produced farm tools and blades become widely available at low prices
Agricultural mechanization changes the demand for farm tools themselves
Skills survive in blade-producing regions and as sword smiths

099.timelineClose: It became cheaper to 'buy' than to 'make,' and more common to 'replace' than to 'repair.' However, hand-forged blades are still highly valued today, and the skill lives on.
099.trivia: Japanese blade-producing regions (such as Sakai, Seki, Tsubame-Sanjo) are where the techniques of village blacksmiths accumulated and developed into industries. Even if individual blacksmiths disappeared, their skills are sold worldwide as regional brands.
099.lineageText: Blacksmith → Factory Production (survives as blade-producing regions and sword smiths)
